docs.title: Home
docs.text: The phase relations of the H₂O–NaCl system at 250 bar, corresponding approximately to hydrostatic pressure at 2.5 km water depth. The diagram shows regions where liquid, vapour and halite coexist, alongside the density of the single-phase fluid, indicated by shades of blue. At seawater salinity (dashed line), phase separation begins at approximately 388 °C, producing a low-salinity vapour and a more saline liquid. The pronounced change in fluid density and the appearance of coexisting phases illustrate how temperature and salinity influence the behaviour of hydrothermal fluids.

docs.title: xThermo
docs.text:
Phase relations and thermodynamic properties of H₂O–NaCl fluids from 0 to 1000 °C and 1 to 5000 bar, after Driesner & Heinrich (2007) and Driesner (2007). A C++ library for simulation codes, with a Python interface for NumPy and Matplotlib.

docs.title: What xThermo computes
docs.text:
• Phase relations

    Explore the stability and coexistence of liquid, vapour and halite across temperature, pressure and salinity, including the critical curve.

  • Fluid properties

    Calculate density, specific enthalpy, heat capacity, viscosity and thermodynamic derivatives for H₂O–NaCl fluids and their coexisting phases.

  • Python for science

    Evaluate individual states or entire NumPy arrays, and create phase diagrams and thermodynamic property maps using Python.

  • C++ for simulation codes

    Integrate xThermo into C++ simulation software through its CMake interface, with support for robust error handling and parallel applications.

  • Pure water and NaCl

    Calculate properties of pure water using IAPS-84 or IAPWS-95, as well as solid and liquid NaCl.

  • Checked against the literature

    The numerical implementation has been systematically verified against published reference data. See Model and limitations for details.

docs.title: Seawater heated at 250 bar
docs.text:
The figure follows the evolution of seawater as it is heated at a constant pressure of 250 bar, corresponding to the dashed salinity line in the phase diagram above. Below approximately 388 °C, seawater remains a single liquid phase. At higher temperatures, it separates into a low-salinity vapour and a concentrated brine. As heating continues, the vapour fraction increases and the remaining liquid becomes progressively enriched in NaCl. At approximately 449 °C, the liquid phase disappears and halite precipitates. Further heating produces a mixture of vapour and solid halite. This sequence illustrates how phase separation can redistribute water and salt in hydrothermal systems, particularly near mid-ocean ridges. Python code for both figures 
"""Homepage figures: the H2O-NaCl phase diagram at 250 bar with the density of the single-phase fluid, and seawater
heated at 250 bar.

Writes hero_desktop.png, hero_mobile.png and seawater_250bar.png to docs/assets/img (or the directory given as the
first argument or in $XTHERMO_FIGURE_DIR). Needs xthermo and matplotlib.
"""
import os

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

import _style as st

st.apply()
OUT = st.outdir(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "assets", "img"))

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
P = 250e5                      # Pa
X_SEAWATER = 0.032             # kg/kg (3.2 wt% NaCl)

# fluid density on a T-X grid; the multiphase regions are drawn over it by plot_slice
T = np.linspace(1, 999, 400) + 273.15
X = np.logspace(-5, 0, 400)
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, T[:, None], P, X[None, :], errors="nan")
section = sw.Slice_constP(P)

# seawater heated at 250 bar: where it separates into brine and vapour, and how salty each phase is
Tp = np.linspace(300, 600, 601) + 273.15
q = xthermo.tpx(sw, Tp, P, X_SEAWATER, errors="nan")
two_phase = q.has("vapour") & q.has("liquid")
vapour_mass = np.where(q.ok, q.S_v * q.Rho_v / q.Rho, np.nan)
tc = Tp - 273.15
T_SPLIT = tc[two_phase].min()       # °C, where seawater starts to separate into vapour and brine
T_HALITE = tc[two_phase].max()      # °C, above it vapour + halite


def phase_diagram(figsize, fontsize, labels, note, note_xy):
    with plt.rc_context({"font.size": fontsize}):
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
        ax.set_xscale("log")
        field = xthermo.plot_property(ax, s, "Rho", x="X", y="T", cmap=st.OCEAN, vmin=0, vmax=1300, colorbar=False)
        xthermo.plot_slice(ax, section, x="X", y="T", points=False)
        ax.axvline(X_SEAWATER * 100, color=st.CORAL, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (5, 3)), zorder=5)
        ax.set_xlim(1e-3, 100)
        ax.set_ylim(0, 1000)
        ax.set_xlabel("bulk salinity (wt% NaCl)")
        ax.set_ylabel("temperature (°C)")
        cb = fig.colorbar(field["mesh"], ax=ax, pad=0.015, fraction=0.04, aspect=30)
        cb.set_label("density of the single-phase fluid (kg/m³)")
        cb.outline.set_visible(False)
        for x, y, text, colour in labels:
            ax.text(x, y, text, color=colour, ha="center", va="center", zorder=6)
        ax.text(X_SEAWATER * 100 * 1.12, 965, "seawater", color=st.CORAL, ha="left", va="top", zorder=6,
                fontweight="bold")
        ax.plot([X_SEAWATER * 100], [T_SPLIT], "o", ms=fontsize * 0.7, mfc=st.CORAL, mec="white", mew=1.5, zorder=7)
        ax.annotate(note, (X_SEAWATER * 100, T_SPLIT), xytext=note_xy, color="white", ha="right", va="center",
                    zorder=7, fontsize=fontsize * 0.9, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color="white", lw=1))
        ax.set_title("H₂O–NaCl at 250 bar")
    return fig


desktop = phase_diagram((11, 5.2), 11, [
    (1.0, 870, "vapour + liquid", st.NAVY),
    (3, 600, "vapour + halite", st.INK),
    (68, 120, "liquid\n+ halite", st.NAVY),
    (5e-3, 110, "liquid-like fluid", "white"),
    (5e-3, 620, "vapour-like fluid", st.INK),
], f"seawater separates into\nvapour + brine at ≈{T_SPLIT:.0f} °C", (0.9, 250))
desktop.text(0.0, -0.02, st.CREDIT, fontsize=8, color=st.MUTED, transform=desktop.transFigure)
desktop.savefig(os.path.join(OUT, "hero_desktop.png"))

mobile = phase_diagram((6.2, 6.4), 14, [
    (1.0, 870, "V + L", st.NAVY),
    (3, 600, "V + H", st.INK),
    (52, 110, "L+H", st.NAVY),
    (6e-3, 120, "liquid-like", "white"),
], f"splits at\n≈{T_SPLIT:.0f} °C", (0.9, 260))
mobile.savefig(os.path.join(OUT, "hero_mobile.png"))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.0))
ax.axvspan(T_SPLIT, T_HALITE, color="#ddeef3", lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.axvspan(T_HALITE, tc[-1], color="#eeeeee", lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.semilogy(tc, np.where(q.has("liquid"), q.X_l * 100, np.nan), color=st.NAVY, lw=2.2, label="liquid (brine)")
ax.semilogy(tc, np.where(q.has("vapour"), q.X_v * 100, np.nan), color=st.CORAL, lw=2.2, label="vapour")
ax.set_ylabel("salinity of the phase (wt% NaCl)")
ax.set_xlabel("temperature (°C)")
ax.set_xlim(tc[0], tc[-1])
ax.legend(loc="upper right", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.86))
ax2 = ax.twinx()
ax2.spines["right"].set_visible(True)
ax2.plot(tc, vapour_mass * 100, color=st.TEAL, lw=1.4, ls="--")
ax2.set_ylim(0, 100)
ax2.set_ylabel("vapour mass fraction (%)", color=st.TEAL)
ax2.tick_params(axis="y", colors=st.TEAL)
ax.text((T_SPLIT + T_HALITE) / 2, 0.25, "vapour\n+ brine", ha="center", va="center", color=st.INK)
ax.text((T_HALITE + tc[-1]) / 2, 0.25, "vapour + halite", ha="center", va="center", color=st.INK)
ax.text((tc[0] + T_SPLIT) / 2, 0.25, "liquid", ha="center", va="center", color=st.INK)
ax.set_title("Seawater (3.2 wt% NaCl) heated at 250 bar")
fig.text(0.0, -0.03, st.CREDIT, fontsize=7.5, color=st.MUTED, transform=fig.transFigure)
fig.savefig(os.path.join(OUT, "seawater_250bar.png"))
print("hero_desktop.png hero_mobile.png seawater_250bar.png written to", os.path.abspath(OUT))

The script uses a few shared style settings from docs/gallery/_style.py.

docs.title: Quick start
Development
docs.text:
xThermo is developed and maintained by the Seafloor Modeling group at the GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel.

Zhikui Guo developed the original C++ library, including the water and NaCl backends and Python bindings, building on earlier MATLAB implementations of the Driesner formulation developed at GEOMAR.

Lars Rüpke leads the project and maintains its scientific development.

xThermo supports research on hydrothermal systems and is used, among other applications, in OpenFOAM-based hydrothermal flow simulations with HydrothermalFoam.

docs.title: How to cite
docs.text:
xThermo implements the H₂O–NaCl formulations developed by Thomas Driesner and Christoph Heinrich. When publishing results obtained with xThermo, please cite both foundational papers:

Driesner, T. & Heinrich, C.A. (2007). The system H₂O–NaCl. Part I: Correlation formulae for phase relations in temperature–pressure–composition space from 0 to 1000 °C, 0 to 5000 bar, and 0 to 1 XNaCl. Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, 71, 4880–4901. doi:10.1016/j.gca.2006.01.033

Driesner, T. (2007). The system H₂O–NaCl. Part II: Correlations for molar volume, enthalpy, and isobaric heat capacity from 0 to 1000 °C, 1 to 5000 bar, and 0 to 1 XNaCl. Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, 71, 4902–4919. doi:10.1016/j.gca.2007.05.026

Please also cite the pure-water formulation used in your calculations:

  • IAPS-84: Haar, L., Gallagher, J.S. & Kell, G.S. (1984). NBS/NRC Steam Tables. Hemisphere, Washington; and Kestin, J. & Sengers, J.V. (1986). J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data 15, 305. doi:10.1063/1.555772
  • IAPWS-95: Wagner, W. & Pruß, A. (2002). J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data 31, 387–535. doi:10.1063/1.1461829

For calculations involving brine viscosity, please cite Klyukin, Yu.I., Lowell, R.P. & Bodnar, R.J. (2017). Fluid Phase Equilib. 433, 193–205. doi:10.1016/j.fluid.2016.11.002. All references are listed on Model and limitations.

To cite the software itself, use xThermo, GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel, https://github.com/lruepke/xThermo, and specify the version used (xthermo.__version__). A software DOI is planned.

docs.title: Command-line tool
docs.text:
xThermal evaluates the models from the shell: single states, profiles, grids and files of points. It is installed with the library in <prefix>/bin/. Every example on this page runs in the documentation's test suite exactly as printed.

xThermal <program> [options]
xThermal <program> -h          help for one program
xThermal -h | -v               general help, version
Program Purpose thermo evaluate states from T–p–X or H–p–X input lutgen, lutinfo, lookup, lut2vtu build, inspect, query and convert adaptive lookup tables (below)

docs.title: A first example
docs.text:
Seawater-like brine (10 wt% NaCl) at 300 °C and 300 bar:

xThermal thermo -D0 -VPTX -T300 -P300E5 -X0.1

H2O-NaCl
T=300 deg.C = 573.15 K, P=300 bar, X=10 wt% NaCl, H=1.21693e+06 J/kg
  phase: Liquid
  Rho=849.034 [kg/m^3]
  H=1.21693e+06 [J/kg]
  Cp=4407.72 [J/kg/K]
  Mu=0.000114076 [Pa S]
  dRhodT=-1.3541 [kg/m3/K]
  dRhodP=1.06661e-06 [kg/m3/Pa]
  Isothermal compressibility=1.25627e-09 [1/Pa]
  Isobaric expansivity=0.00159487 [1/K]

The values are those of the Python and C++ interfaces (xthermo.tpx(sw, 573.15, 300e5, 0.1)).

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
Temperature: °C on the command line, K in files

-T and the temperature ranges of -R are in degrees Celsius. Input files (-G) and every output file (CSV and VTK) use kelvin.

Quantity Options Unit temperature -T, -R °C temperature -G files; CSV and VTK output K pressure -P, -R, files, output Pa (300 bar = 300E5) salinity -X, -R, files, output kg NaCl / kg fluid, 0–1 (seawater: 0.032) specific enthalpy -H, -R, files, output J/kg

docs.title: Options of thermo
docs.text:
A value follows its option letter directly or after a space: -P300E5 and -P 300E5 are the same.

Option Meaning -D n required: 0 = single points or a file of points, 1 = profile, 2 = grid, 3 = 3-D grid -V vars required: the varying variables, in order (see the table below) -T, -P, -X, -H fixed values of the variables not in -V (-T and -H exclude each other) -R min/step/max… ranges of the variables in -V, in the same order (-D1 to -D3) -G file file of points (-D0) -O file output file (Output) -F fluid H2O-NaCl (default), H2O or NaCl -B model water model: IAPS84 (default) or IAPWS95 -t n threads; effective only in a library built with -DXTHERMO_OPENMP=ON, otherwise ignored -p show a progress bar (for interactive use on a terminal) -n accepted for compatibility; has no effect -h, -v help, version -D -V Needs 0 PTX or PHX (any order) -T/-H, -P, -X, or a file -G 1 T, P, X or H the two other variables fixed, -R with 3 values, -O 2 PT, PX, TX, PH or HX (either order) the third variable fixed, -R with 6 values 3 PTX or PHX (any order) -R with 9 values; H₂O–NaCl only

Ranges. -Rmin/step/max gives evenly spaced values from min to max, both included: (max − min)/step + 1 points, rounded down, with the spacing adjusted to fit. min must be smaller than max, and the step positive and not larger than max − min. -R1/100/1000 gives 10 values, 111 K apart.

With -F H2O the salinity is 0 and with -F NaCl it is 1, so -X is not needed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Single point from enthalpy:

xThermal thermo -D0 -VPHX -H1500E3 -P316E5 -X0.032

A file of points. Three numbers per line in the order of -V, temperature in kelvin; blank lines are skipped:

points.txt
300E5 573.15 0.1
250E5 673.15 0.032

xThermal thermo -D0 -VPTX -Gpoints.txt -Opoints_result.csv

Profiles at fixed pressure and salinity, in temperature and in enthalpy:

xThermal thermo -D1 -VT -P250E5 -X0.032 -R1/1/1000 -OT_profile.csv
xThermal thermo -D1 -VH -P250E5 -X0.032 -R100E3/10E3/3000E3 -OH_profile.csv

and in pressure and salinity:

xThermal thermo -D1 -VP -T350 -X0.032 -R5E5/5E5/1000E5 -OP_profile.csv
xThermal thermo -D1 -VX -T350 -P250E5 -R0/0.01/1 -OX_profile.csv

Grids: temperature–salinity at 250 bar, and pressure–temperature for seawater:

xThermal thermo -D2 -VTX -R1/5/1000/0/0.01/1 -P250E5 -OTX_250bar.vtk
xThermal thermo -D2 -VPT -R1E5/10E5/1000E5/1/5/800 -X0.032 -OPT_seawater.vtk

A 3-D grid in pressure, temperature and salinity:

xThermal thermo -D3 -VPTX -R100E5/100E5/1000E5/100/50/1000/0/0.05/1 -OPTX.vtk

Pure water with IAPWS-95, and pure NaCl:

xThermal thermo -D0 -VPTX -T380 -P250E5 -FH2O -BIAPWS95
xThermal thermo -D0 -VPTX -T900 -P300E5 -FNaCl

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Mode Output -D0 with -T/-H, -P, -X the property listing on the screen (stdout) -D0 with -G, -D1 a CSV file: -O name, or out_<V>.csv for -G without -O; -D1 requires -O -D2, -D3 a legacy VTK file and a ParaView script (<name>.vtk.py): -O name, or <V>.vtk without -O

CSV files have one row per point. The first columns are T[K], P[Pa], X[kg/kg], then the phase compositions, the phase region (Phase[index], Phase[name]), and the bulk and phase densities, enthalpies, heat capacities, viscosities and saturations. For H₂O–NaCl the saturations Sl[m3/m3], Sv, Sh are volume fractions; for pure water, Sl[kg/kg], Sv are mass fractions. The bulk heat capacity and viscosity of multiphase states follow the definitions on Model and limitations (the viscosity column of a two-phase point holds a placeholder 1).

A CSV name that does not end in .csv gets .csv appended (result.txt gives result.txt.csv). A grid is always written as .vtk: -Ogrid.csv or -Ogrid gives grid.vtk, with a notice.

docs.title: Exit status and errors
docs.text:
Status Meaning 0 success (also -h and -v) 1 the evaluation failed: an input outside the model's range, a state the model cannot evaluate, an unreadable or malformed input file, an unwritable output file 2 the command line cannot be interpreted: an unknown program, option, fluid or water model; a missing or malformed value; a missing required option; an invalid -D, -V or -R; both -T and -H

Errors and warnings go to stderr, results to stdout. A failing point in a file, profile or grid stops the run (status 1, no output file).

# above the model's 1000 °C: exit status 1
xThermal thermo -D0 -VPTX -T1100 -P300E5 -X0.1 || echo "exit status $?"
# -X missing: exit status 2
xThermal thermo -D0 -VPTX -T300 -P300E5 || echo "exit status $?"

The command-line tool checks T, p and X against the model's range before evaluating. Inputs outside the published model domain are rejected there, including pressures below 1 bar, which the library itself would evaluate (see Domain, input checks and errors).

docs.title: Lookup tables
docs.text:
lutgen builds an adaptive lookup table of the properties over a 2-D or 3-D region, lutinfo describes it, lookup evaluates points from it, and lut2vtu converts it for ParaView:

xThermal lutgen -D2 -VXT -R0/0.05/1/100/10/500 -P250E5
xThermal lutinfo lut_constP_XT_6.bin
xThermal lookup lut_constP_XT_6.bin -D0 -VTPX -T300 -P250E5 -X0.1

lutgen writes its files into the current directory, with names from the table type and refinement level (lut_constP_XT_<level>.bin, one file per property, and a .vtu file); it does not use -O. -L sets the minimum refinement level (default 4). Interpolated values from a table are not covered by the verification of the model.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• -t has an effect only in a library built with OpenMP; -n has no effect.
  • Error messages for a failed evaluation give the library's explanation but not the input point.

docs.title: Gallery
docs.text:
The following examples illustrate the phase relations and thermodynamic properties of H₂O–NaCl fluids calculated with xThermo. They highlight phenomena relevant to hydrothermal systems, including phase separation, boiling during decompression, and fluid behaviour near the critical point.

All calculations follow the formulations of Driesner & Heinrich (2007) and Driesner (2007), using the IAPS-84 water backend.

Each figure can be reproduced using the accompanying Python code, which is also included in the documentation's automated tests.

Additional examples are available on the homepage and in the Python guides to phase diagrams and property maps.

docs.title: The H₂O–NaCl phase diagram
docs.text:
The phase relations of the H₂O–NaCl system form a three-dimensional structure in temperature–pressure–composition space. The two-dimensional phase diagrams shown below represent sections through this structure.

The vapour–liquid coexistence region is bounded by two surfaces representing the compositions of the coexisting liquid (dark grey) and vapour (light grey). These surfaces converge along the critical curve (red), where the distinction between liquid and vapour disappears.

At lower pressures, the vapour–liquid–halite three-phase surface connects the compositions of the coexisting phases (blue and orange). Below this surface, vapour and halite coexist (purple). On the salt-rich side of the diagram, the halite liquidus (green) separates the single-phase liquid region from the liquid–halite coexistence region.

The salinity axis is linear, making the very low NaCl concentrations of the vapour phase difficult to distinguish near the pure-water end of the diagram. The following two-dimensional sections use a logarithmic salinity scale to illustrate these regions in greater detail.

Python code 
import warnings
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
from matplotlib.colors import to_hex
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)
sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")

# ── VLH surface (V→L side and L→H side) ──────────────────────────────────
nT = 80
nT_high = nT // 3
T_high  = H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH + (sw.Tmax_VLH() - H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH) * 0.95
T_vlh   = np.append(np.linspace(H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH, T_high, nT - nT_high),
                    np.linspace(T_high, sw.Tmax_VLH(), nT_high))
P_vlh   = np.array(sw.P_VLH(T_vlh))
Xl_vlh, Xv_vlh = np.array(sw.X_VLH(T_vlh, P_vlh))

n_log, n_lin = 20, 40
nX = n_log + n_lin
TT_vlh = np.tile(T_vlh, (nX, 1))
PP_vlh = np.tile(P_vlh, (nX, 1))
XX_V2L = np.zeros_like(TT_vlh)
XX_L2H = np.zeros_like(TT_vlh)
for j in range(len(T_vlh)):
    XX_V2L[:, j] = np.append(
        10 ** np.linspace(np.log10(max(Xv_vlh[j], 1e-10)), np.log10(0.01), n_log),
        np.linspace(0.01, Xl_vlh[j], n_lin))
    XX_L2H[:, j] = np.linspace(Xl_vlh[j], 1.0, nX)

# ── VH surface ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
nP = 60
T_vh = np.linspace(H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH, sw.Tmax_VLH(), nT)
P_vlh2 = np.array(sw.P_VLH(T_vh))
TT_vh = np.tile(T_vh, (nP, 1))
PP_vh = np.zeros_like(TT_vh)
np_low = nP // 3
for i in range(len(T_vh)):
    p_low = sw.pmin() + (P_vlh2[i] - sw.pmin()) * 0.1
    PP_vh[:, i] = np.append(np.linspace(sw.pmin(), p_low, np_low),
                            np.linspace(p_low, P_vlh2[i], nP - np_low))
XX_VH = np.array(sw.X_VH(TT_vh.ravel(), PP_vh.ravel())).reshape(TT_vh.shape)

# ── Halite liquidus ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
TT_lh = np.tile(T_vh, (nP, 1))
PP_lh = np.zeros_like(TT_lh)
for i in range(len(T_vh)):
    PP_lh[:, i] = np.linspace(P_vlh2[i], 2500e5, nP)
XL_LH = np.array(sw.X_HaliteLiquidus(TT_lh.ravel(), PP_lh.ravel())).reshape(TT_lh.shape)

# ── VL surfaces ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
pb_l = sw.PhaseBoundary_VL_DeformLinear(H2ONaCl.Liquid)
pb_v = sw.PhaseBoundary_VL_DeformLinear(H2ONaCl.Vapor)

# ── Critical curve ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
T_crit = np.linspace(sw.get_pWater().T_critical(), sw.Tmax(), 80)
p_crit, X_crit = np.array(sw.P_X_Critical(T_crit))

# ── Plot ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(12, 9))
ax  = fig.add_subplot(111, projection='3d', facecolor='None')
legend = []   # 3-D surfaces give no usable legend handles: one coloured swatch per surface

def surf(TT, PP, XX, color, label):
    ax.plot_surface(XX * 100, TT - 273.15, PP / 1e5,
                    color=color, alpha=0.45, linewidth=0)
    ax.plot_wireframe(XX * 100, TT - 273.15, PP / 1e5,
                      color=color, lw=0.4)
    legend.append(Patch(fc=color, ec=color, alpha=0.6, label=label))

surf(TT_vlh, PP_vlh, XX_V2L,  'steelblue', 'VLH (V side)')
surf(TT_vlh, PP_vlh, XX_L2H,  'orange',    'VLH (L+H side)')
surf(TT_vh,  PP_vh,  XX_VH,   'purple',    'VH surface')
surf(TT_lh,  PP_lh,  XL_LH,   'limegreen', 'Halite liquidus')

for pb, color, label in [(pb_l, 'black', 'VL liquid'), (pb_v, 'gray', 'VL vapor')]:
    T2 = np.array(pb.T); P2 = np.array(pb.p); X2 = np.array(pb.X)
    ax.plot_surface(X2 * 100, T2 - 273.15, P2 / 1e5, color=color, alpha=0.3, linewidth=0)
    ax.plot_wireframe(X2 * 100, T2 - 273.15, P2 / 1e5, color=color, lw=0.4)
    legend.append(Patch(fc=color, ec=color, alpha=0.4, label=label))

ax.plot(X_crit * 100, T_crit - 273.15, p_crit / 1e5, color='red', lw=2)
legend.append(Line2D([], [], color='red', lw=2, label='Critical curve'))
ax.plot(Xv_vlh * 100, T_vlh - 273.15, P_vlh / 1e5, color='red',   lw=1)
ax.plot(Xl_vlh * 100, T_vlh - 273.15, P_vlh / 1e5, color='green', lw=1)

ax.set_xlabel('Salinity (wt% NaCl)', fontsize=10, labelpad=8)
ax.set_ylabel('Temperature (°C)',    fontsize=10, labelpad=8)
ax.set_zlabel('Pressure (bar)',      fontsize=10, labelpad=8)
ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_ylim(0, 1000); ax.set_zlim(0, 2500)
ax.view_init(elev=25, azim=-145)
ax.set_title(r'H$_2$O–NaCl phase boundaries in T–p–X space', fontsize=13, pad=12)
ax.legend(handles=legend, loc='upper left', fontsize=9)
ax.set_box_aspect(None, zoom=0.88)   # leaves room for the axis labels
plt.show()

docs.title: How the phase diagram changes with depth
docs.text:
The three-dimensional phase diagram can be explored through sections at constant pressure. The figure compares temperature–salinity sections at 100, 250, 400 and 1000 bar, corresponding approximately to hydrostatic pressures at depths of 1, 2.5, 4 and 10 km in seawater.

At 100 bar, seawater begins to separate into vapour and saline liquid at approximately 312 °C. Between 341 and 771 °C, vapour coexists with halite, indicating that the liquid brine has disappeared and salt has precipitated.

As pressure increases, phase separation begins at progressively higher temperatures: approximately 388 °C at 250 bar, 447 °C at 400 bar and 688 °C at 1000 bar.

The vapour–liquid–halite three-phase equilibrium is restricted to pressures below approximately 390 bar. At higher pressures, the phase relations change accordingly, while the halite liquidus on the salt-rich side of the diagram is comparatively insensitive to pressure.

Python code 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

import _style as st                              # fonts and colours of the documentation figures (docs/gallery)

st.apply()
sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
pressures = [100e5, 250e5, 400e5, 1000e5]        # Pa

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(13, 4.4), sharey=True, layout="constrained")
handles = {}
for ax, p in zip(axes, pressures):
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    h = xthermo.plot_slice(ax, sw.Slice_constP(p), x="X", y="T", points=False)
    handles.update(h)
    ax.set_xlim(1e-3, 100)                       # wt% NaCl
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1000)                         # °C
    ax.set_title(f"{p / 1e5:.0f} bar", loc="center")
    ax.axvline(3.2, color=st.CORAL, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (5, 3)))   # seawater
    if ax is not axes[0]:
        ax.set_ylabel("")
# one legend entry for the three-phase assemblage (its temperature differs between the panels)
vlh = [k for k in handles if k.startswith("V+L+H")]
handles = {k: v for k, v in handles.items() if k not in vlh} | {"V+L+H (a line in T–X)": handles[vlh[0]]}
fig.legend(handles.values(), handles.keys(), loc="outside lower center", ncol=7, fontsize="small")
fig.suptitle("The H₂O–NaCl phase diagram at four pressures (dashed: seawater, 3.2 wt% NaCl)", x=0.01, ha="left",
             color=st.NAVY, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()

docs.title: Coexisting brine and vapour
docs.text:
When H₂O–NaCl fluids undergo vapour–liquid phase separation, the coexisting phases can differ substantially in density and salinity. The liquid phase becomes enriched in NaCl, while the vapour generally contains much less dissolved salt.

The figure illustrates the temperature dependence of the density and salinity of coexisting liquid and vapour at pressures of 250, 400, 600 and 1000 bar.

At each pressure, the liquid and vapour branches converge at the critical curve, where the distinction between the two phases disappears. Away from the critical curve, density differences can exceed 1000 kg/m³, providing a strong driving force for gravitational phase separation. The salinity contrast can span several orders of magnitude.

Increasing pressure generally shifts the critical conditions towards higher temperatures and allows greater concentrations of NaCl in the vapour phase.

At 250 bar, the vapour–liquid region is interrupted between approximately 449 and 716 °C by vapour–halite equilibrium, where halite precipitates and no liquid phase is present.

The figure is restricted to temperatures below 800 °C. At higher temperatures, the published vapour-composition correlation requires an additional implementation choice, as discussed under Implementation choices and formulation differences.

Python code 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

import _style as st                              # fonts and colours of the documentation figures (docs/gallery)

st.apply()
sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
T = np.linspace(380, 800, 421) + 273.15          # K; up to 800 °C (see the text)
colours = {250e5: st.CORAL, 400e5: st.TEAL, 600e5: "#1f6f9a", 1000e5: st.NAVY}

fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.6), layout="constrained")
for p, colour in colours.items():
    # compositions of the coexisting liquid and vapour; a bulk salinity between them lies in the two-phase field
    x_l = np.array(sw.XL_VL(T, np.full_like(T, p)))
    x_v = np.array(sw.XV_VL(T, np.full_like(T, p)))
    s = xthermo.tpx(sw, T, p, 0.5 * (x_l + x_v), errors="nan", absent="nan")
    two_phase = s.ok & s.has("liquid") & s.has("vapour") & ~s.has("halite")
    rho_l = np.where(two_phase, s.Rho_l, np.nan)
    rho_v = np.where(two_phase, s.Rho_v, np.nan)
    label = f"{p / 1e5:.0f} bar"
    ax.plot(T - 273.15, rho_l, color=colour, lw=2, label=label)
    ax.plot(T - 273.15, rho_v, color=colour, lw=2, ls="--")
    bx.semilogy(T - 273.15, np.where(two_phase, 100 * s.X_l, np.nan), color=colour, lw=2, label=label)
    bx.semilogy(T - 273.15, np.where(two_phase, 100 * s.X_v, np.nan), color=colour, lw=2, ls="--")

ax.set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)")
ax.set_ylabel("density (kg/m³)")
ax.set_title("Density: brine (solid) and vapour (dashed)")
ax.legend(fontsize="small")
bx.set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)")
bx.set_ylabel("salinity (wt% NaCl)")
bx.set_title("Salinity: brine (solid) and vapour (dashed)")
bx.legend(fontsize="small", loc="lower right")
fig.suptitle("Coexisting brine and vapour in the vapour + liquid field of H₂O–NaCl", x=0.01, ha="left",
             color=st.NAVY, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()

docs.title: Rising seawater: boiling or condensation
docs.text:
As hydrothermal fluids rise towards the seafloor, decreasing pressure can lead to phase separation. Whether vapour forms or liquid condenses depends on the initial thermodynamic state of the fluid.

The figure illustrates the isenthalpic decompression of three fluids with seawater salinity, initially at 500 bar and temperatures of 380, 420 and 450 °C. Their evolution is calculated at constant specific enthalpy, representing an idealised ascent without heat exchange or changes in kinetic and potential energy.

The two cooler fluids initially occupy liquid-like states. During decompression, they enter the vapour–liquid region at approximately 191 and 260 bar, respectively. Vapour is generated, and its proportion increases as pressure decreases.

The hottest fluid begins in a vapour-like state near the critical curve. As it decompresses, it enters the two-phase region from the vapour-rich side at approximately 331 bar, causing a small amount of saline liquid to condense rather than vapour to form.

At 50 bar, all three fluids coexist as vapour and brine at approximately 266 °C.

These idealised paths demonstrate the contrasting phase-separation behaviour of rising hydrothermal fluids. Natural hydrothermal circulation also involves heat exchange with surrounding rocks and fluid mixing, which are not represented in this example.

Python code 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

import _style as st                              # fonts and colours of the documentation figures (docs/gallery)

st.apply()
sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
X = 0.032                                        # seawater salinity, kg/kg
p = np.geomspace(500e5, 50e5, 300)               # decompression from 500 to 50 bar, Pa

# where seawater is a single phase or vapour + liquid, in temperature and pressure
T_grid = np.linspace(200, 500, 301) + 273.15
P_grid = np.geomspace(40e5, 550e5, 300)
grid = xthermo.tpx(sw, T_grid[None, :], P_grid[:, None], X, errors="nan")

fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.6), layout="constrained")
ax.set_yscale("log")
xthermo.plot_phases(ax, grid, x="T", y="P", legend=False)
ax.invert_yaxis()                                # pressure decreases upwards, as on the way to the seafloor

for T0, colour in [(380, st.NAVY), (420, st.TEAL), (450, st.CORAL)]:
    start = xthermo.tpx(sw, T0 + 273.15, p[0], X)            # the fluid at depth
    path = xthermo.hpx(sw, start.H, p, X, errors="nan")       # same specific enthalpy at every pressure
    ax.plot(path.T - 273.15, p / 1e5, color=colour, lw=2.2, label=f"starts at {T0} °C, 500 bar")
    boiling = path.has("vapour") & path.has("liquid")
    w_vapour = np.where(boiling, path.S_v * path.Rho_v / path.Rho, np.nan)   # vapour mass fraction (two phases only)
    bx.plot(p / 1e5, 100 * w_vapour, color=colour, lw=2.2)
    i = np.flatnonzero(boiling)[0]
    ax.plot(path.T[i] - 273.15, p[i] / 1e5, "o", ms=7, mfc=colour, mec="white", mew=1.5)

ticks = [50, 100, 200, 300, 500]                 # bar
ax.set_yticks(ticks, [str(t) for t in ticks])
ax.set_title("Path in temperature and pressure")
ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize="small")
ax.text(300, 300, "single-phase fluid", ha="center", fontsize="small")
ax.text(300, 75, "vapour + liquid", ha="center", fontsize="small")
ax.text(470, 70, "vapour\n+ halite", ha="center", fontsize="small")

bx.set_xscale("log")
bx.set_xticks(ticks, [str(t) for t in ticks])
bx.invert_xaxis()
bx.annotate("starts as a vapour-like fluid:\na brine condenses", (325, 70), xytext=(240, 88), fontsize="small",
            color=st.CORAL, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=st.CORAL))
bx.text(150, 8, "start as liquid-like fluids: they boil", fontsize="small", color=st.INK)
bx.set_xlabel("Pressure (bar)")
bx.set_ylabel("vapour mass fraction (%)")
bx.set_ylim(0, 100)
bx.set_title("Vapour mass fraction once two phases coexist")
fig.suptitle("Seawater rising from 500 bar at constant specific enthalpy (no heat exchange)", x=0.01, ha="left",
             color=st.NAVY, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()

docs.title: Water near its critical point
docs.text:
Near the critical point, the thermodynamic properties of water change rapidly with temperature and pressure. Above the critical pressure (approximately 220.5 bar), water transitions continuously between liquid-like and vapour-like states without crossing a phase boundary.

The figure compares density and isobaric heat capacity calculated with IAPS-84 and IAPWS-95 at pressures of 230, 250, 300 and 400 bar.

At pressures just above the critical pressure, the heat capacity exhibits a pronounced maximum, reflecting the strong temperature dependence of enthalpy in this region. With increasing pressure, this maximum becomes broader and shifts towards higher temperatures. These properties are important for understanding heat transport in hydrothermal systems.

Both water formulations predict similar behaviour across the investigated conditions. The largest differences occur near the heat-capacity maximum at 230 bar, where the calculated peak values differ by approximately 10%.

The IAPS-84 formulation has a restricted validity range immediately surrounding the critical point, and calculations in this region require particular care. Further discussion is provided under Applicability and known limitations.

Python code 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2O

import _style as st                              # fonts and colours of the documentation figures (docs/gallery)

st.apply()
models = {"IAPS-84": H2O.cIAPS84(), "IAPWS-95": H2O.cIAPWS95()}
T = np.linspace(330, 480, 1501) + 273.15         # K, steps of 0.1 K
colours = {230e5: st.CORAL, 250e5: st.TEAL, 300e5: "#1f6f9a", 400e5: st.NAVY}

fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.4), layout="constrained")
for p, colour in colours.items():
    for (name, water), ls in zip(models.items(), ["-", ":"]):
        s = xthermo.tpx(water, T, p, errors="nan")
        label = f"{p / 1e5:.0f} bar" if name == "IAPS-84" else None
        ax.semilogy(T - 273.15, s.Cp / 1e3, color=colour, ls=ls, lw=1.8, label=label)
        bx.plot(T - 273.15, s.Rho, color=colour, ls=ls, lw=1.8, label=label)
ax.set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)")
ax.set_ylabel("isobaric heat capacity (kJ/(kg K))")
ax.set_title("Heat capacity above the critical pressure")
ax.legend(title="solid: IAPS-84, dotted: IAPWS-95", fontsize="small", title_fontsize="small")
bx.set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)")
bx.set_ylabel("density (kg/m³)")
bx.set_title("Density")
fig.suptitle("Pure water near its critical point (374 °C; 220.5 bar IAPS-84, 220.6 bar IAPWS-95)", x=0.01, ha="left", color=st.NAVY,
             fontweight="bold")
plt.show()

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: xThermo is a C++ library with a Python interface. Python users build and install the package xthermo with pip; C++ users build and install the library with CMake. Both compile the library from source, which takes a few minutes.

docs.title: From source (current)
docs.text:
You need Python ≥ 3.10, a C/C++ compiler (gcc ≥ 11 or Apple clang) and make. pip takes CMake and SWIG from PyPI if they are not installed, and builds GSL from the official, checksum-verified release.

git clone https://github.com/lruepke/xThermo.git
cd xThermo
pip install .                 # or: pip install ".[plotting]" to add matplotlib

Use any environment you like (venv, conda, …). NumPy is installed as a dependency; Matplotlib is only needed for the plotting helpers.

Check the installation:

import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, 573.15, 300e5, 0.1)      # T [K], p [Pa], X [kg/kg]
print(xthermo.__version__, s.phase_name, s.Rho)

The former package name still works: from xThermal import H2ONaCl gives the same modules.

docs.text:

A package on PyPI is planned: prebuilt wheels for Linux and macOS, installed with

pip install xthermo

It is not yet published, so this command does not work yet; install from source as above. The licensing of binary packages, which contain GSL (GPL) and Triangle (non-commercial licence), is being settled first; see About.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
Dependency Required Notes C++ compiler (gcc ≥ 11 or Apple clang) yes the code is compiled as C++11 CMake ≥ 3.18 yes GSL 2.x yes from the system, or built from source by CMake (see below) SWIG ≥ 4 and Python ≥ 3.10 with headers for the Python modules skip with -DXTHERMO_PYTHON=OFF PROST 4.1 bundled the IAPS-84 water backend; compiled automatically

GSL from your package manager:

brew install gsl              # macOS
sudo apt install libgsl-dev   # Debian/Ubuntu
conda install -c conda-forge gsl

For a GSL in a non-standard location add -DGSL_ROOT_DIR=<prefix>. Without a system GSL, add -DXTHERMO_BUNDLED_GSL=ON: CMake then downloads the official GSL 2.8 release from ftp.gnu.org, checks its SHA-256 checksum and builds it. For offline builds, point -DXTHERMO_GSL_ARCHIVE=<path to gsl-2.8.tar.gz> to a local copy of the same archive.

docs.title: Build and install
docs.text:
From the repository root:

cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=install
cmake --build build -j
cmake --install build

The build type is Release unless -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE is given. Options:

Option Default Description XTHERMO_PYTHON ON Build the Python modules (SWIG) XTHERMO_BUNDLED_GSL OFF Build the pinned GSL release from source instead of using the system GSL XTHERMO_OPENMP OFF Use OpenMP for batch and lookup-table evaluation BUILD_SHARED_LIBS OFF Build the C++ library as a shared library XTHERMO_BUILD_TESTS OFF Build the developer test programs (ctest)

cmake --install creates:

install/
├── bin/xThermal                 # command-line tool
├── include/xThermo/             # C++ headers
├── lib/libxThermal.a            # C++ library (lib64/ on some Linux distributions)
├── lib/cmake/xThermo/           # CMake package: find_package(xThermo)
└── API/python/cp3.13/           # Python modules; the name follows the Python version used by CMake
    ├── xthermo/                 # __init__.py, H2O.py, NaCl.py, H2ONaCl.py, the compiled modules, ...
    └── xThermal/                # compatibility name

To use these Python modules without pip, set PYTHONPATH=/path/to/xThermo/install/API/python/cp3.13.

docs.text:
find_package(xThermo REQUIRED)
target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE xThermo::xThermal)

Point CMake to the installation with -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/path/to/xThermo/install (or export xThermo_DIR=/path/to/xThermo/install). More in the C++ API overview.

docs.title: Model, verification and limitations
docs.text:
xThermo implements the phase relations and thermodynamic properties of the H₂O–NaCl system following the formulations of Driesner & Heinrich (2007) and Driesner (2007). The model covers temperatures from 0 to 1000 °C, pressures from 1 to 5000 bar, and compositions ranging from pure water to pure NaCl.

This page describes the scientific formulation, its numerical verification in xThermo, and relevant implementation choices and limitations.

docs.title: Phase relations
docs.text:
Driesner & Heinrich (2007) describe the phase relations of the H₂O–NaCl system as functions of temperature, pressure and NaCl mole fraction. Their correlations define the phase boundaries, including the critical curve, halite liquidus, vapour–liquid–halite equilibrium, and the melting, boiling and sublimation curves of NaCl. They also describe the compositions of coexisting liquid and vapour phases.

Together, these relations determine the stable phase assemblage for a given temperature, pressure and bulk composition.

The Gallery illustrates the phase relations at different pressures and in three dimensions.

docs.title: Volumetric and thermal properties
docs.text:
Driesner (2007) describes the molar volume, specific enthalpy and isobaric heat capacity of H₂O–NaCl fluids using a corresponding-temperature approach. In this formulation, the properties of saline fluids are related to those of pure water through separate temperature-scaling functions for volume and enthalpy. The isobaric heat capacity is obtained from the temperature derivative of the enthalpy.

The original formulation uses the IAPS-84 equation of state for pure water, which remains the reference backend in xThermo. An alternative implementation using IAPWS-95 is also available.

In regions where the scaled temperature falls outside the applicable range of the pure-water formulation, extrapolations are required. These are discussed below under implementation differences and limitations.

The properties of halite are described by separate correlations.

docs.title: Viscosity
docs.text:
The dynamic viscosity of H₂O–NaCl fluids is calculated following Klyukin et al. (2017), using a corresponding-temperature approach based on the viscosity of pure water.

Pure-water viscosity is evaluated using the IAPWS (2008) formulation with the IAPWS-95 backend and the NBS/NRC Steam Tables correlation implemented in PROST with the IAPS-84 backend.

docs.title: Water backends
docs.text:
Driesner (2007) uses the IAPS-84 formulation for the thermodynamic properties of pure water. xThermo retains IAPS-84 as its reference backend and also supports IAPWS-95 as an alternative.

Backend Formulation Pure-water implementation IAPS84 IAPS-84 (Haar et al., 1984; Kestin & Sengers, 1986) PROST 4.1 IAPWS95 IAPWS-95 (Wagner & Pruß, 2002) xThermo implementation

The choice of water backend affects the calculated thermodynamic properties of H₂O–NaCl fluids because Driesner's corresponding-temperature formulation relies on pure-water properties.

IAPS-84 provides consistency with the original formulation, while IAPWS-95 offers an alternative based on the more recent pure-water equation of state. The two backends generally give similar results, although differences can become more pronounced near phase boundaries and the critical region.

The published temperature, pressure and composition limits of the H₂O–NaCl correlations apply independently of the selected water backend.

docs.title: Model domain
docs.text:
The H₂O–NaCl correlations of Driesner & Heinrich (2007) and Driesner (2007) cover temperatures from 0 to 1000 °C, pressures from 1 to 5000 bar, and the complete composition range from pure water to pure NaCl.

While the published correlations use NaCl mole fraction, xThermo's public API uses NaCl mass fraction (kg/kg). For example, seawater with 3.2 wt% NaCl is specified as X = 0.032.

The corresponding limits reported by the H₂O–NaCl class are Tmin() = 273.16 K, Tmax() = 1273.15 K, pmin() = 1e5 Pa, and pmax() = 5e8 Pa.

Not all inputs outside the published domain are rejected automatically. See Input validation and error handling for details.

docs.title: What was compared
docs.text:
The numerical implementation of xThermo has been systematically verified against the published formulations and supplementary data of Driesner & Heinrich (2007) and Driesner (2007).

The verification includes:

  • Published reference tables: All ten supplementary tables were evaluated, comprising 29,680 values across 24 property comparisons. Of these, 13 comparisons reproduce the published values to their reported precision. Differences in the remaining comparisons have been investigated and documented, including differences arising from implementation choices, numerical behaviour near phase boundaries and inconsistencies between individual tabulated values and the published equations. A small number of marginal discrepancies remain unresolved.
  • Published equations: Explicit analytical correlations were independently evaluated and compared with both the published tables and xThermo.
  • SoWat: Selected results were compared with SoWat 0.2 (2009), providing an additional reference implementation of the Driesner formulation.
  • Pure-water formulations: The IAPS-84 and IAPWS-95 implementations were checked against their respective published reference values and available independent calculations.
  • Internal consistency: Thermodynamic derivatives and the consistency between temperature-based (T–p–X) and enthalpy-based (H–p–X) evaluations were examined.

These comparisons are maintained as automated regression tests in the development repository.

docs.title: What the agreement means
docs.text:
The comparisons demonstrate how closely xThermo reproduces the published Driesner formulations and reference data. They provide confidence in the numerical implementation and help identify differences associated with particular correlations, implementation choices or numerical conditions.

The agreement with reference calculations should be distinguished from the physical accuracy of the underlying thermodynamic model. Driesner & Heinrich (2007) and Driesner (2007) assessed their correlations against available experimental data and discussed the associated uncertainties and limits of applicability.

For example, Driesner (2007) reports density uncertainties of approximately 0.1–0.2% at low temperatures and pressures, and heat-capacity deviations reaching approximately 10% at elevated temperatures and salinities. These estimates characterize the published formulation rather than the numerical precision of xThermo.

docs.title: Scope of verification
docs.text:
The verification described above focuses primarily on the phase relations, density and enthalpy correlations of Driesner & Heinrich (2007) and Driesner (2007), together with the underlying pure-water formulations.

Some aspects of the implementation have not yet been evaluated to the same extent:

  • The viscosity correlation of Klyukin et al. (2017) for saline fluids and the IAPS-84 pure-water viscosity implementation.
  • The thermodynamic properties of halite and liquid NaCl.
  • Independent comparisons of heat capacities and density derivatives with experimental measurements.
  • Systematic verification of phase identification throughout the full temperature–pressure–composition domain, beyond the states represented in the published reference tables.
  • Additional reference comparisons for IAPS-84 beyond its published check values.

The IAPWS-95 backend represents an alternative implementation of the corresponding-temperature formulation. Since Driesner's reference tables were generated using IAPS-84, they do not provide a direct reference for results obtained with IAPWS-95.

These distinctions define the present scope of the verification effort and identify opportunities for further assessment.

docs.title: Implementation choices and formulation differences
docs.text:
xThermo follows the formulations of Driesner & Heinrich (2007) and Driesner (2007), with a small number of documented adaptations inherited from earlier GEOMAR implementations or introduced during development.

Comparisons with the published equations, supplementary tables and other implementations, including SoWat and ProBrine (Klyukin et al., 2020), have identified differences in the treatment of selected thermodynamic properties and phase relations.

The following sections describe three cases that have been examined in detail: isobaric heat capacity, liquid enthalpy at high temperatures and low pressures, and vapour composition above the melting point of NaCl. For each case, the implementation choice and its numerical consequences are documented.

Some differences concern regions where the published formulation requires extrapolation or leaves implementation details unspecified. The current treatment is retained pending further scientific evidence.

docs.title: Heat capacity
docs.text:
In xThermo, the isobaric heat capacity is calculated as the temperature derivative of the specific enthalpy at constant pressure and composition, following Eq. 27 of Driesner (2007):

cP = (∂h/∂T)p,x

SoWat 0.2 and ProBrine apply an additional factor of 1/(1 + x) to the published heat-capacity expression, where x denotes the NaCl mole fraction. This correction is not included in Eq. 27 of Driesner (2007), although SoWat identifies it as an omission in the original publication.

Applying this factor to heat capacity without a corresponding modification of enthalpy changes the relationship between the two properties. xThermo therefore retains the published equation to preserve consistency between enthalpy and its temperature derivative.

The resulting heat capacities differ from SoWat and ProBrine by approximately 1% at seawater salinity, 9% at 26 wt% NaCl and 23% at 58 wt% NaCl. The physical justification for the additional factor remains unresolved and would require further assessment against experimental data.

docs.title: Liquid enthalpy of hot brines at low pressure
docs.text:
At temperatures above approximately 600 °C and pressures below 390 bar, the corresponding-temperature approach of Driesner (2007) may map saline liquid states into the vapour region of the pure-water formulation, where the enthalpy correlation cannot be applied directly.

To evaluate liquid enthalpy in this region, xThermo uses a smooth extrapolation developed at GEOMAR, following the approach used for density in Driesner (2007). The extrapolation is continuous at its upper pressure boundary, and the resulting heat capacity remains consistent with the temperature derivative of enthalpy.

Comparisons with the supplementary tables of Driesner (2007) show differences of up to approximately 3%, with a median difference of 0.8%. The treatment used to generate the published tabulated values in this region is not specified in the paper.

Because these conditions require extrapolation beyond the underlying correlations, the available comparisons do not establish which treatment more accurately represents the physical properties of saline liquids.

docs.title: Vapour composition above the melting point of NaCl
docs.text:
Above the melting point of NaCl (800.7 °C), Eq. 15 of Driesner & Heinrich (2007) contains a parameter whose value is not explicitly defined for this temperature range.

xThermo assigns a value of unity to this parameter, consistent with the published phase-boundary conditions. SoWat uses a different, temperature-dependent treatment that is not specified in the published paper.

As a result, the calculated NaCl concentration in the vapour phase differs between the two implementations. Relative to SoWat, xThermo predicts approximately 1.3% lower concentrations at 810 °C, 6–13% lower concentrations at 850–900 °C, and differences of up to approximately 24% at 1000 °C. At pressures below 300 bar, the corresponding vapour concentrations are generally small, approximately 0.01–0.2 wt% NaCl.

Below 800.7 °C, xThermo reproduces the vapour compositions reported in the supplementary tables of Driesner & Heinrich (2007).

Available experimental data do not presently provide a basis for selecting between these treatments.

docs.title: Other implementation details
docs.text:
Several additional implementation choices originate from earlier GEOMAR developments or were introduced during the development of xThermo.

Property or correlation Implementation detail Low-temperature density correction The correction term D(T) in Eq. 13 of Driesner (2007) is omitted because it can shift the corresponding temperature below the freezing point of pure water. The resulting density differences are generally below 0.01% above approximately 50 °C and reach 0.18% at lower temperatures near halite saturation. Molar mass of water xThermo uses 18.015268 g/mol instead of 18.015 g/mol in Driesner (2007). The resulting differences in density and composition conversions are approximately 0.0015% or less. Low-pressure density extrapolation The implementation of Eq. 17 of Driesner (2007) differs slightly from the published expression, whose notation is ambiguous. Density differences reach approximately 0.16–0.46% near boiling at 1–15 bar. High-temperature density extrapolation The implementation of Eq. 18 of Driesner (2007) differs slightly from the published expression, with density differences of approximately 0.06% or less in the investigated high-temperature, low-pressure region. High-temperature liquid composition Above 800.7 °C, the liquid branch of the vapour–liquid coexistence surface uses a slightly different pressure reference, resulting in composition differences of approximately 10−5 or less. Pure-water viscosity extrapolation With the IAPS-84 backend, the PROST water-viscosity correlation is evaluated beyond its nominal upper temperature limit of 900 °C. These results should be considered extrapolations.

These differences are documented to distinguish implementation choices from the published formulation. Their significance depends on the thermodynamic conditions and properties of interest.

docs.title: Multiphase properties
docs.text:
In multiphase regions, xThermo provides the thermodynamic properties of the individual coexisting phases as well as selected properties of the bulk fluid mixture.

Phase-specific quantities, including density (Rho_l, Rho_v), enthalpy (H_l, H_v), heat capacity (Cp_l, Cp_v), viscosity (Mu_l, Mu_v) and composition (X_l, X_v), are evaluated at the equilibrium composition of each phase.

Bulk quantities require additional definitions because their values may depend on phase proportions, phase equilibrium and the treatment of phase transitions. The following table summarizes the conventions currently used in xThermo.

Property Single-phase state Multiphase state Phase fractions (S_l, S_v, S_h) 1 for the phase present Volume fractions of the coexisting phases in the H₂O–NaCl model. Bulk density (Rho) Density of the phase Volume-weighted average of the phase densities: ρ = ∑i Si ρi. Bulk specific enthalpy (H) Specific enthalpy of the phase Mass-weighted average of the phase enthalpies: h = (∑i Si ρi hi)/ρ. Heat capacity (Cp) Isobaric heat capacity of the phase, cP = (∂h/∂T)p,x. In two-phase regions, the mass-weighted average of the individual phase heat capacities, evaluated at fixed phase proportions and compositions. In V+L+H, not computed (0 is a placeholder). Isothermal compressibility (IsothermalCompressibility) Isothermal compressibility of the phase. In two-phase H₂O–NaCl regions, calculated from the pressure dependence of bulk density at constant temperature and bulk composition, allowing the phases to re-equilibrate. In V+L+H, not computed (0 is a placeholder). Thermal expansivity (IsobaricExpansivity) Isobaric thermal expansivity of the phase. Not computed (0 is a placeholder). Density derivatives (dRhodT, dRhodP) Temperature and pressure derivatives of phase density. Not computed (0 values are placeholders); use phase-specific properties where available. Viscosity (Mu) Dynamic viscosity of the phase. No general effective multiphase viscosity model is implemented. The returned value depends on phase assemblage and evaluation method (see below).

Phase-fraction convention: In the H₂O–NaCl model, S_l, S_v and S_h represent volume fractions. The pure-water classes use a different convention: S_v represents vapour mass fraction (quality). These quantities must not be interchanged without conversion.

docs.title: Heat capacity in multiphase regions
docs.text:
In two-phase regions, xThermo reports a phase-weighted heat capacity:

cP,bulk = (∑i Si ρi cP,i)/ρ

This quantity represents the heat capacity at fixed phase proportions and compositions, often referred to as a frozen heat capacity. It does not include latent heat associated with phase transitions or changes in the equilibrium compositions of the coexisting phases.

Consequently, it generally differs from the equilibrium temperature derivative of the bulk enthalpy,

(∂H/∂T)p,X

which includes changes in phase proportions and compositions.

At fixed pressure, the temperature of a V+L+H equilibrium state is constrained by the three-phase equilibrium. xThermo does not compute a bulk heat capacity for these states; the returned value of zero is a placeholder, not a physical heat capacity.

For example, at 400 °C, 250 bar and 10 wt% NaCl, xThermo returns a phase-weighted Cp of approximately 9.2 kJ/(kg K), whereas the temperature derivative of bulk enthalpy is approximately 31 kJ/(kg K):

import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
dT = 0.01                                            # K
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, 673.15 + np.array([-dT, 0.0, dT]), 250e5, 0.10)
print(s.phase_name[1])                               # V+L
print(s.Cp[1] / 1e3)                                 # frozen: 9.2 kJ/(kg K)
print((s.H[2] - s.H[0]) / (2 * dT) / 1e3)            # equilibrium (dH/dT): 31 kJ/(kg K)

docs.title: Isothermal compressibility in multiphase regions
docs.text:
In two-phase regions, xThermo calculates the isothermal compressibility from the bulk density:

κT = −(1/ρ)(∂ρ/∂p)T,X

The calculation accounts for changes in phase proportions and equilibrium compositions as pressure varies.

For three-phase vapour–liquid–halite states, this quantity is not evaluated. A returned value of zero indicates that the property has not been computed, rather than zero physical compressibility.

The pure-water classes also leave the bulk compressibility uncomputed for two-phase states obtained through enthalpy-based evaluation (H–p–X).

docs.title: Viscosity in multiphase regions
docs.text:
The effective viscosity of a multiphase fluid depends on its flow characteristics and cannot generally be determined from the thermodynamic properties of the individual phases alone.

xThermo does not implement a constitutive model for effective multiphase viscosity. In two-phase H₂O–NaCl regions, the bulk Mu field currently contains a placeholder value of 1. In three-phase states, and in two-phase pure-water states evaluated from enthalpy-based input, it contains a volume-fraction-weighted average of liquid and vapour viscosities, excluding halite.

Neither convention should be interpreted as an effective viscosity for multiphase flow calculations. Applications should use the phase-specific viscosities (Mu_l, Mu_v) together with an appropriate multiphase-flow model.

Absent phases: Fields belonging to a phase that is not present retain zero in the C++ structure and classic interface; xthermo.tpx and xthermo.hpx can return NaN instead (absent="nan"). See Evaluating states.

docs.title: Input validation and error handling
docs.text:
The published model domain and the input range enforced at runtime are not identical:

Input condition Current behaviour Temperature above 1000 °C OutOfRangeError Enthalpy above the upper model limit OutOfRangeError Non-finite inputs, non-positive pressure or negative salinity InvalidInputError Pressure below 1 bar Not rejected automatically; results are extrapolations outside the published domain. Pressure above 5000 bar Behaviour depends on the water backend; IAPS-84 may return extrapolated values, while IAPWS-95 raises OutOfRangeError. NaCl mass fraction above 1 Not rejected automatically; returned results have no physical interpretation.

Accepting an input numerically does not imply that its result lies within the published validity range. Check input units and model applicability before evaluation.

When evaluation fails, the library raises a typed exception rather than returning a previous or partial state. C++ exceptions derive from xThermal::xThermalBaseError; Python exceptions from xthermo.EvaluationError. These include InvalidInputError, OutOfRangeError, NotConvergedError and NotAvailableError. C++ callers can use tryUpdateState_TPX and tryUpdateState_HPX to obtain an EvaluationStatus without throwing.

For arrays, xthermo.tpx and xthermo.hpx raise the first error by default (errors="raise"). With errors="nan", failed points are set to NaN and per-point outcomes are reported in a Status array, while valid points are preserved. See Errors and status.

When an individual property cannot be evaluated at an otherwise valid state, that property may be NaN while the remaining properties are valid. For example, the IAPS-84 pure-water viscosity has its own validity restrictions (above 5000 bar; above 3500 bar for T > 150 °C; above 3000 bar for T > 600 °C), which also affect brine viscosity derived from it.

Some phase-boundary helper functions have a different convention: outside their supported temperature ranges, they may print a warning and return zero (for example, X_Critical).

docs.title: Limitations of the published correlations
docs.text:
The formulations of Driesner & Heinrich (2007) and Driesner (2007) provide a broad description of the H₂O–NaCl system. As with any empirical formulation, their applicability depends on the experimental data and assumptions underlying the correlations.

Several regions require particular consideration:

  • Extrapolated conditions: Brine densities at low pressures near boiling, and the density and enthalpy of hot saline liquids above approximately 600 °C and below 390 bar, involve extrapolations of the published correlations. Conditions below 1 bar lie outside the published model domain.
  • Highly saline liquids at low pressure: In a restricted region near halite saturation, at pressures of approximately 1–5 bar and temperatures of 10–100 °C, the published density correlation can yield negative isothermal compressibility. Although the associated variation in calculated density is small, negative compressibility is not thermodynamically consistent with a stable homogeneous phase. xThermo retains the published density correlation and calculates derivatives consistently with it.
  • Critical region: Predictions near the critical point of water require particular care because of the limitations and increasing sensitivity of the underlying pure-water formulations. These effects can also influence dilute saline fluids through the corresponding-temperature approach.
  • High-temperature phase compositions and enthalpy: The vapour-composition treatment above 800.7 °C and the extrapolation of liquid enthalpy at high temperature and low pressure are discussed under Implementation choices and formulation differences.

docs.title: Known numerical issues
docs.text:
The following numerical issues have been identified in specific regions of the model domain. They are documented here to help users assess their relevance to particular applications.

Phase-diagram geometry

Some functions used to construct two-dimensional phase diagrams (Slice_constP and Slice_constT) have known geometric inaccuracies:

  • At pressures below approximately 221 bar, a narrow part of the vapour–liquid region may be omitted from enthalpy–salinity diagrams at very low salinity (below approximately 0.13 wt% NaCl).
  • In isothermal diagrams, the liquid–halite region may extend below the three-phase pressure into the vapour–halite field. The current plotting routines generally cover this overlap with the correctly drawn vapour–halite region.
  • Isothermal sections below 374 °C may contain a spurious critical point at zero salinity.

These issues concern the construction of phase-region polygons and do not affect direct thermodynamic state evaluations through tpx or hpx.

Thermodynamic property evaluation

  • Pure-water saturation conditions: Very close to the saturation pressure of pure water, the IAPS-84 backend may produce inconsistent phase labels and densities or small discontinuities in calculated properties. The IAPWS-95 backend may fail to converge at the saturation boundary.
  • IAPWS-95 at low temperatures and high pressures: For certain saline compositions, the corresponding-temperature transformation reaches conditions outside the supported range of the pure-water formulation. This can prevent evaluation at low temperatures or near the upper pressure boundary of 5000 bar. The IAPS-84 backend can evaluate these conditions.
  • Low-pressure density derivatives: Near boiling at approximately 1–5 bar, calculated pressure derivatives of brine density can differ significantly from numerical derivatives of the density correlation. The calculated density itself is unaffected.
  • High-temperature density with IAPWS-95: In the low-pressure extrapolation region, small numerical discontinuities may occur in density and its temperature derivative.
  • Enthalpy extrapolation below 1 bar: A known implementation issue can affect calculated liquid enthalpies at pressures below the published model domain, or when liquid properties are requested at conditions where no stable liquid phase exists.

docs.title: Under investigation
docs.text:
Two related questions concerning pure NaCl near its melting point remain under investigation.

Enthalpy-based evaluation near melting

For pure NaCl, enthalpies between those of solid halite and liquid NaCl at the melting temperature correspond to coexistence of the two phases. In this region, enthalpy-based evaluation (hpx) may return a successful result whose calculated enthalpy differs from the requested value.

For example, at 250 bar, an input enthalpy of 1.031 MJ/kg produces a liquid–halite state at approximately 806.9 °C with a returned enthalpy of 0.807 MJ/kg.

Until this behaviour is resolved, enthalpy-based evaluations of pure NaCl within the melting interval should be treated with caution.

Enthalpy of solid and liquid NaCl

The enthalpy of solid halite is calculated using a separate correlation, while the enthalpy of liquid NaCl is obtained from the Driesner (2007) fluid formulation at pure-NaCl composition.

At 1 bar, the calculated enthalpy difference at melting is approximately 0.25 MJ/kg. The consistency of the reference states and the agreement of this difference with published enthalpy-of-fusion data have not yet been established.

Further examination is required to determine whether the observed behaviour reflects a reference-state inconsistency, a numerical issue or another aspect of the formulation.

docs.title: C++ API overview
docs.text: xThermo is a C++ library; the Python package and the command-line tool are built on the same classes. This guide covers the stable public interface: constructing a model, evaluating states, handling errors, and using the library from several threads. The model itself, its verification and its limitations are described on Model and limitations.

docs.title: Installing the library
docs.text:
Build and install xThermo with CMake (details and options on Installation):

cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=install
cmake --build build -j
cmake --install build

The installation (here /path/to/xThermo/install) contains the headers in include/xThermo/, the library libxThermal in lib/ (lib64 on some Linux distributions), the command-line tool xThermal in bin/, and a CMake package in lib/cmake/xThermo/.

docs.title: Using xThermo in a CMake project
docs.text:
find_package(xThermo) provides the target xThermo::xThermal, which carries the include directory and the GSL dependency. A complete project has two files:

CMakeLists.txt
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.18)
project(my_app LANGUAGES CXX)

find_package(xThermo REQUIRED)

add_executable(my_app main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE xThermo::xThermal)
main.cpp
#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    // H2O-NaCl with the IAPS-84 water model
    xThermal::H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl brine("IAPS84");
    // T [K], p [Pa], X [kg/kg]
    xThermal::ThermodynamicProperties s = brine.UpdateState_TPX(300 + 273.15, 300e5, 0.1);
    std::cout << brine.phase_name(s.phase) << ", " << s.Rho << " kg/m3\n";   // Liquid, 849.034 kg/m3
}

Configure with the installation prefix in CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH, then build and run:

cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/path/to/xThermo/install
cmake --build build
./build/my_app

The test suite builds this project against a fresh installation.

Compiling without CMake

The library needs the GSL. With a system GSL (gsl-config in the PATH):

g++ -std=c++11 -I/path/to/xThermo/install/include/xThermo $(gsl-config --cflags) \
    -o my_app main.cpp -L/path/to/xThermo/install/lib -lxThermal $(gsl-config --libs)

If xThermo was built with -DXTHERMO_BUNDLED_GSL=ON, the GSL is installed with it: use -I/path/to/xThermo/install/lib/xThermo/gsl/include and -L/path/to/xThermo/install/lib/xThermo/gsl/lib -lgsl -lgslcblas instead of gsl-config. CMake does this for you.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
Class Model Construction xThermal::H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl H₂O–NaCl (Driesner & Heinrich 2007; Driesner 2007) cH2ONaCl brine("IAPS84") or ("IAPWS95"): the water model used inside xThermal::PROST::cIAPS84 pure water, IAPS-84 cIAPS84 water; xThermal::IAPWS95::cIAPWS95 pure water, IAPWS-95 cIAPWS95 water; xThermal::NaCl::cNaCl pure NaCl cNaCl salt("IAPS84");

Including H2ONaCl.h makes all four available. All derive from xThermal::cxThermal, so a function can take any model as cxThermal&. An unknown water-model name throws NotImplementedError at construction. "IAPS84" is the reference: the H₂O–NaCl correlations were fitted with it (see Water backends).

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
All functions use SI units, with temperature in kelvin:

Quantity Unit temperature T K pressure p Pa salinity X kg NaCl / kg fluid (mass fraction, 0–1) specific enthalpy H J/kg density kg/m³ heat capacity J/(kg K) viscosity Pa s

Tmin(), Tmax(), pmin() and pmax() give the range a model declares: for H₂O–NaCl 273.16–1273.15 K and 1e5–5e8 Pa. Which inputs outside it are rejected is listed under Errors and threads.

docs.title: In this guide
docs.text:
• Evaluating states: T–p–X and H–p–X evaluation, single points and batches, the result fields
  • Errors and threads: exceptions, status codes, thread safety, OpenMP
  • Phase region: the phase of a state without evaluating its properties
  • Phase boundaries: the critical curve, the three-phase surface, coexisting compositions

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
When a state cannot be evaluated, UpdateState_TPX and UpdateState_HPX throw an exception derived from xThermal::xThermalBaseError (itself a std::exception; what() gives the message, code() the error code). The library does not return a previous state, a partial result or default values instead.

Exception Cause EvaluationStatus InputError (a ValueError) non-finite T, H, p or X; p ≤ 0; X < 0 InvalidInput OutOfRangeError outside the range in which the model evaluates, e.g. T above 1273.15 K for H₂O–NaCl OutOfRange SolutionError a numerical solution failed, e.g. IAPWS-95 water exactly at its saturation pressure NotConverged NotImplementedError, NotAvailableError not provided for this model or state, e.g. H–p–X for pure NaCl NotAvailable other xThermalBaseError (e.g. ValueError) any other error reported by the library Failed 
#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>

using namespace xThermal;

int main()
{
    H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl brine("IAPS84");
    ThermodynamicProperties props;
    try {
        brine.UpdateState_TPX(props, 1100 + 273.15, 300e5, 0.1);         // above the model's 1000 °C
    } catch (const OutOfRangeError& e) {
        std::cout << "out of range\n";
    } catch (const xThermalBaseError& e) {                               // any other failure
        std::cout << evaluation_status_name(evaluation_status(e.code())) << ": " << e.what() << "\n";
    }
}

docs.title: Status codes
docs.text:
tryUpdateState_* and the batch functions evaluate_* report the same failures as an EvaluationStatus (Evaluating states). evaluation_status(e.code()) converts an exception's code, and evaluation_status_name(status) gives its name ("OutOfRange" for EvaluationStatus::OutOfRange). In the batch results, status[i] holds the value as an integer:

Value EvaluationStatus Python (xthermo.Status) 0 Ok Ok 1 InvalidInput InvalidInput 2 OutOfRange OutOfRange 3 NotConverged NotConverged 4 NotAvailable NotAvailable 5 Failed Failed

Errors that are not evaluation failures (for example std::bad_alloc) are not converted into a status; they propagate from every function.

docs.title: Input checks
docs.text:
Every evaluation rejects non-finite inputs, p ≤ 0 and X < 0 (InputError), and H₂O–NaCl temperatures above 1273.15 K (OutOfRangeError). Other inputs outside the published model domain (0–1000 °C, 1–5000 bar, X 0–1) are not all rejected: pressures below 1 bar, and X above 1, are evaluated as extrapolations. Check inputs against the domain where it matters; Domain, input checks and errors has the full list.

A single property that cannot be evaluated at an otherwise valid state is NaN, and the other properties remain valid (Result fields).

docs.title: Threads
docs.text:
A model object is not thread-safe. Code that evaluates states concurrently needs one model object per thread. Independent objects share no state and give the same results as a serial evaluation. Construct a new object per thread rather than copying one:

#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

using namespace xThermal;

int main()
{
    std::vector<double> T = {300 + 273.15, 350 + 273.15, 400 + 273.15, 450 + 273.15};   // K
    std::vector<double> rho(T.size());
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < T.size(); i++)
        threads.emplace_back([i, &T, &rho]() {
            H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl brine("IAPS84");        // one model per thread
            rho[i] = brine.UpdateState_TPX(T[i], 300e5, 0.1).Rho;
        });
    for (auto& t : threads) t.join();
    for (double r : rho) std::cout << r << " kg/m3\n";
}

MPI ranks have their own objects anyway. In OpenMP code of your own, create the model inside the parallel region.

Internal OpenMP (optional). A library built with -DXTHERMO_OPENMP=ON can evaluate the vector functions (evaluate_* and the vector UpdateState_*) in parallel: model.set_num_threads(n) sets the number of threads for that object. It creates one model per thread itself and gives the same results as a serial evaluation. The default is 1 thread, and the build option is off by default. Without it, set_num_threads has no effect and get_num_threads() returns 1. In a program that is already parallel (a simulator with MPI or its own threads), keep the internal threading off.

docs.title: Pressure of the V+L+H surface
docs.text:
P_VLH returns the pressure on the three-phase V+L+H surface for a given temperature.

#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>

using namespace xThermal;

int main()
{
    H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl eos("IAPS84");

    int N = 100;
    double T_min = H2ONaCl::T_MIN_VLH;
    double T_max = H2ONaCl::T_MAX_VLH;
    double dT = (T_max - T_min) / (N - 1);

    std::cout << "T(°C)    P_VLH(bar)\n";
    for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
        double T = T_min + i * dT;   // K
        double P = eos.P_VLH(T);     // Pa
        std::cout << T - 273.15 << "    " << P / 1e5 << "\n";
    }
}

docs.text:
#include "H2ONaCl.h"

docs.title: Liquid and vapour compositions on the V+L+H surface
docs.text:
#include "H2ONaCl.h"
