docs.title: Phase region
docs.text:
findPhaseRegion_TPX returns the phase region index without computing all thermodynamic properties.

#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>

using namespace xThermal;

int main()
{
    H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl eos("IAPS84");

    double T = 400 + 273.15;   // K
    double p = 200e5;           // Pa  (200 bar)
    double X = 0.032;           // kg/kg  (3.2 wt% NaCl)

    PhaseRegion region = eos.findPhaseRegion_TPX(T, p, X);
    std::string name = eos.phase_name(region);

    std::cout << "Phase region: " << name << " (index " << region << ")\n";
}

docs.title: Phase region names
docs.text:
Names returned by phase_name for H₂O–NaCl states:

Name Enum value Description Liquid SinglePhase_L Single liquid phase. Single-phase "liquid-like" and "vapour-like" fluid above the critical curve are also reported as Liquid. Vapor SinglePhase_V Single vapour phase V+L TwoPhase_VL Vapour–liquid coexistence L+H TwoPhase_LH Liquid–halite coexistence V+H TwoPhase_VH Vapour–halite coexistence V+L+H ThreePhase_VLH Three-phase coexistence (reached through the H–p–X flash)

For pure water, the names of the water backend are used instead, for example Supercritical and Sup.crit. liquid, and V+L(water) in the two-phase region. This applies to the pure-water classes and also to cH2ONaCl at X = 0, which evaluates pure water directly.

docs.title: Phase name from an UpdateState result
docs.text:
#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>

using namespace xThermal;

int main()
{
    H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl eos("IAPS84");
    ThermodynamicProperties props;
    eos.UpdateState_TPX(props, 400 + 273.15, 250e5, 0.1);
    std::cout << eos.phase_name(props.phase) << "\n";   // V+L
}

docs.title: Evaluating states
docs.text:
A state is given by temperature, pressure and bulk salinity (T–p–X), or by specific enthalpy, pressure and salinity (H–p–X). Every model offers the same functions:

Function Input On failure UpdateState_TPX(props, T, p, X), UpdateState_HPX(props, H, p, X) one state; fills props throws (see Errors and threads) UpdateState_TPX(T, p, X), UpdateState_HPX(H, p, X) one state; returns the properties throws tryUpdateState_TPX(props, T, p, X, &message), tryUpdateState_HPX(...) one state returns an EvaluationStatus evaluate_TPX(T, p, X), evaluate_HPX(H, p, X) vectors of points records a status per point UpdateState_TPX(T, p, X), UpdateState_HPX(H, p, X) with vectors vectors of points throws at the first failing point

For pure water and pure NaCl, X is ignored (it may be omitted).

docs.title: One state
docs.text:
#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>

using namespace xThermal;

int main()
{
    H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl brine("IAPS84");

    ThermodynamicProperties props;
    // T [K], p [Pa], X [kg/kg]: seawater at 400 °C, 250 bar
    brine.UpdateState_TPX(props, 400 + 273.15, 250e5, 0.032);

    std::cout << brine.phase_name(props.phase) << "\n"          // V+L
              << "bulk density " << props.Rho << " kg/m3\n"     // 194.068
              << "liquid: " << props.Rho_l << " kg/m3, X_l = " << props.X_l << "\n"
              << "vapour: " << props.Rho_v << " kg/m3, X_v = " << props.X_v << "\n"
              << "vapour volume fraction " << props.S_v << "\n";

    // the same state from its enthalpy: T is a result
    ThermodynamicProperties same = brine.UpdateState_HPX(props.H, 250e5, 0.032);
    std::cout << "T = " << same.T - 273.15 << " °C\n";          // 400
}

Each call resets the result object, so no value of a previous call survives in props.

docs.title: Without exceptions
docs.text:
tryUpdateState_TPX and tryUpdateState_HPX evaluate the same state but return its outcome instead of throwing. On failure the inputs are kept, every other number is NaN, the phase is Unknown, and the optional message receives the library's explanation:

#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

using namespace xThermal;

int main()
{
    H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl brine("IAPS84");
    ThermodynamicProperties props;
    std::string message;

    EvaluationStatus status = brine.tryUpdateState_TPX(props, 1100 + 273.15, 300e5, 0.1, &message);
    if (status != EvaluationStatus::Ok)
        std::cout << evaluation_status_name(status) << "\n";   // OutOfRange: above 1000 °C
    std::cout << props.Rho << "\n";                              // nan
}

The statuses are listed under Errors and threads.

docs.title: Many states
docs.text:
evaluate_TPX and evaluate_HPX take vectors of equal length (point i is T[i], p[i], X[i]) and never stop at a failing point. The result holds one vector per field, status[i] (0 = ok) and the messages of the failed points in failed_message, in index order:

#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

using namespace xThermal;

int main()
{
    H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl brine("IAPS84");
    // K; the second point is above the model's range
    std::vector<double> T = {300 + 273.15, 2000, 400 + 273.15};
    std::vector<double> p = {300e5, 300e5, 250e5};                 // Pa
    std::vector<double> X = {0.1, 0.1, 0.032};                     // kg/kg

    ThermodynamicPropertiesVector r = brine.evaluate_TPX(T, p, X);
    for (size_t i = 0; i < T.size(); i++)
        std::cout << i << ": status " << r.status[i] << ", Rho " << r.Rho[i] << "\n";
    // statuses 0, 2 (OutOfRange; Rho NaN), 0
    std::cout << r.failed_message.size() << " failed point(s)\n";
}

The vector forms of UpdateState_TPX/UpdateState_HPX evaluate the same points but throw at the first failure. With isMeshGrid = true they evaluate every combination of the three vectors.

docs.title: Result fields
docs.text:
ThermodynamicProperties (and the vectors of ThermodynamicPropertiesVector):

Field Meaning T, p, X, H temperature [K], pressure [Pa], bulk salinity [kg/kg], bulk specific enthalpy [J/kg]; T is a result of H–p–X, H of T–p–X phase phase region, a PhaseRegion; phase_name(phase) gives its name (Phase region) Rho, H, Cp, Mu bulk density [kg/m³], enthalpy, heat capacity [J/(kg K)], viscosity [Pa s] S_l, S_v, S_h phase fractions: volume fractions for H₂O–NaCl; the vapour mass fraction (quality) for the water models X_l, X_v salinity of the liquid and the vapour [kg/kg] Rho_l, Rho_v, Rho_h; H_l, H_v, H_h; Cp_l, Cp_v, Cp_h; Mu_l, Mu_v properties of the liquid, vapour and halite phases dRhodT, dRhodP ∂ρ/∂T [kg/(m³ K)], ∂ρ/∂p [kg/(m³ Pa)]; with _l, _v for the phases IsothermalCompressibility, IsobaricExpansivity (1/ρ) ∂ρ/∂p [1/Pa], −(1/ρ) ∂ρ/∂T [1/K]; with _l, _v for the phases

In a single-phase state, the bulk fields are those of the phase; fields of an absent phase are 0.

Multiphase states: Rho and H are the bulk values of the phase assemblage. The bulk Cp contains no latent heat, the bulk Mu is not a mixture viscosity (use Mu_l and Mu_v), and some bulk derivatives are not computed. The definitions, and what each field holds in each case, are on Model and limitations.

Unavailable properties. A property that cannot be evaluated at an otherwise valid state is NaN while the others are valid: for example the IAPS-84 viscosity outside its validity range (above 3500 bar at more than 150 °C, among others), and brine viscosities that depend on it.

docs.title: Python guide
docs.text:
The Python package xthermo gives you the H₂O–NaCl equation of state of Driesner & Heinrich (2007) and Driesner (2007), pure water (IAPS-84, IAPWS-95) and pure NaCl. You evaluate states on NumPy arrays of any shape and draw phase diagrams and property maps with a few Matplotlib helpers.

import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")                         # H2O-NaCl with the IAPS-84 water backend

T = np.array([300.0, 400.0, 500.0]) + 273.15            # K
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, T, 250e5, 0.032)                    # p = 250 bar in Pa, X = 3.2 wt% NaCl
print(s.phase_name)                                     # ['Liquid' 'V+L' 'V+H']
print(s.Rho)                                            # bulk density, kg/m³
print(s.X_v)                                            # vapour salinity, kg/kg (0 where absent)

docs.title: The models
docs.text:
Module Class System xthermo.H2ONaCl cH2ONaCl("IAPS84"), cH2ONaCl("IAPWS95") H₂O–NaCl; the argument selects the water equation of state xthermo.H2O cIAPS84(), cIAPWS95() pure water xthermo.NaCl cNaCl("IAPS84") pure NaCl (halite and liquid)

The Driesner correlations were fitted with IAPS-84, so "IAPS84" is the reference backend for H₂O–NaCl. "IAPWS95" gives slightly different brine properties; see Model and limitations.

Create a model once and reuse it for all your evaluations. A model object is not meant to be shared between threads; use one per thread.

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
Inputs and outputs are in SI units everywhere:

Quantity Unit temperature T K pressure p Pa (1 bar = 10⁵ Pa) salinity X kg NaCl per kg of fluid, a mass fraction (0.032 = 3.2 wt% NaCl) density kg/m³ specific enthalpy H J/kg heat capacity J/(kg K) viscosity Pa s

The plotting helpers label their axes in °C, bar, wt% NaCl and MJ/kg; their inputs stay in SI.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: pip install . in a clone of the repository installs xthermo with NumPy; pip install ".[plotting]" adds Matplotlib. See Installation. import xthermo loads only the compiled modules; NumPy and Matplotlib are imported when you first use tpx / hpx or a plotting helper.

docs.title: Classic SWIG interface
docs.text: The model classes also expose the library's C++ methods directly, through SWIG. xthermo.tpx and xthermo.hpx are built on them and are usually more convenient. The classic methods remain useful for single points in a loop (they avoid the small overhead of creating a States object) and for existing scripts.

docs.title: Single points
docs.text:
UpdateState_TPX(T, p, X) and UpdateState_HPX(H, p, X) return one ThermodynamicProperties object. Its fields are the same as those of States (see the field table), as plain Python numbers. The water and NaCl models take UpdateState_TPX(T, p).

from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")

props = sw.UpdateState_TPX(300 + 273.15, 300e5, 0.1)       # 300 °C, 300 bar, 10 wt% NaCl
print(sw.phase_name(props.phase), f"{props.Rho:.1f} kg/m³", f"{props.H/1e6:.4f} MJ/kg")

props = sw.UpdateState_HPX(1.5e6, 300e5, 0.05)            # H in J/kg
print(f"{props.T - 273.15:.1f} °C", sw.phase_name(props.phase))

Errors raise Python exceptions: ValueError for invalid or out-of-range input, RuntimeError for a failed solution, NotImplementedError for an unknown backend name. These are the base classes of the more specific exceptions that tpx and hpx raise (Errors and status).

docs.title: 1-D vectors
docs.text:
The same methods take three 1-D lists or arrays of equal length and return an object whose fields are SWIG vectors; convert them with np.array(...). There is no broadcasting: pass every input at full length. If any point fails, the whole call raises and returns nothing.

import numpy as np
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")

T = np.linspace(100 + 273.15, 600 + 273.15, 200)
p = np.full_like(T, 300e5)
X = np.full_like(T, 0.1)

state = sw.UpdateState_TPX(T, p, X)
rho = np.array(state.Rho)
phase = np.array(state.phase)

The equivalent with the NumPy interface is xthermo.tpx(sw, T, 300e5, 0.1), which broadcasts the scalars, returns NumPy arrays and offers errors="nan". Its values are identical to the classic calls.

The vector form of UpdateState_TPX is not available on the pure-water classes in Python; use xthermo.tpx there.

docs.title: Other methods
docs.text:
Every model object also has, among others:

Method Returns phase_name(code) the name of a phase-region code Tmin(), Tmax(), pmin(), pmax() the range the model declares (K, Pa); see Model and limitations for what is checked T_critical(), p_critical() the critical point of water (water models) name() the model's name

The H₂O–NaCl model adds the phase-boundary functions (Phase boundaries) and the sections Slice_constP / Slice_constT (Phase diagrams).

docs.title: The former name xThermal
docs.text:
The package used to be imported as xThermal. That name still works and gives the same modules:

import xthermo
from xThermal import H2ONaCl          # the same module as xthermo.H2ONaCl

print(H2ONaCl is xthermo.H2ONaCl)    # True

New code should use import xthermo.

docs.title: Errors and status
docs.text: A point cannot always be evaluated: the input can be invalid (a NaN, a negative pressure), outside the range of the model (above 1000 °C for H₂O–NaCl), or a numerical solution can fail. tpx and hpx handle this with the errors argument.

docs.title: errors="raise" (the default)
docs.text:
errors="raise" is the default. If any point cannot be evaluated, the call raises an exception for the first such point (in C order). Its message names the point's index and inputs, the library's message and how many further points failed:

import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
T = np.array([300.0, 5000.0, np.nan])                 # K: valid, above the model range, invalid
try:
    xthermo.tpx(sw, T, 250e5, 0.032)
except xthermo.EvaluationError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)                           # OutOfRangeError
    # (1,) Status.OutOfRange {'T': 5000.0, 'p': 25000000.0, 'X': 0.032}
    print(e.index, e.status, e.inputs)
    print(e)                                          # ends in "[1 further failure]"

The exception classes are subclasses of xthermo.EvaluationError and of the matching built-in exception, so existing except ValueError code keeps working:

Exception Also a Status Cause xthermo.InvalidInputError ValueError InvalidInput non-finite T, H or p; p ≤ 0; X < 0 or non-finite X (H₂O–NaCl) xthermo.OutOfRangeError ValueError OutOfRange outside the range in which the model evaluates, e.g. T > 1273.15 K for H₂O–NaCl xthermo.NotConvergedError RuntimeError NotConverged a numerical solution failed, e.g. IAPWS-95 water exactly at its saturation pressure xthermo.NotAvailableError ValueError NotAvailable not implemented for this model or state, e.g. hpx with the pure NaCl model xthermo.EvaluationError Exception Failed any other error reported by the library

Each exception has the attributes index (a tuple; () for scalar input), status, inputs (a dict) and message (the library's message).

docs.title: errors="nan"
docs.text:
With errors="nan" the call never raises for points that cannot be evaluated. Those points are NaN in every number field (their inputs are kept), their phase is Unknown, and their status says why:

import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
T = np.array([300.0, 5000.0, np.nan])
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, T, 250e5, 0.032, errors="nan")

print(s.ok)                                           # [ True False False]
print([xthermo.Status(int(c)).name for c in s.status])   # ['Ok', 'OutOfRange', 'InvalidInput']
print(s.Rho)                                          # [value, nan, nan]
for index, status, message in s.failures:
    print(index, status.name, message[:60])

This is the policy for grids and maps: evaluate everything, then use s.ok to select or mask. The plotting helpers draw points that were not evaluated in grey.

Errors that are not about a point, such as running out of memory or a programming error, are raised in both modes.

docs.title: Status values
docs.text:
xthermo.Status is an integer enumeration; s.status holds these integers (a single Status for scalar input).

Status Value Meaning Ok 0 evaluated InvalidInput 1 invalid input (non-finite, p ≤ 0, X < 0) OutOfRange 2 outside the range in which the model evaluates NotConverged 3 a numerical solution failed NotAvailable 4 not implemented or not available for this model or state Failed 5 any other error of the library

docs.title: Failed points and absent phases
docs.text:
A point that was not evaluated and a phase that is not present at an evaluated point are different things:

Question Test Was the point evaluated? s.ok Is there vapour at an evaluated point? s.has("vapour") (False at failed points) Evaluated, but without vapour? s.ok & ~s.has("vapour")

By default the fields of an absent phase are 0, as in the library; with absent="nan" they are NaN (see Evaluating states). Failed points are NaN in both cases.

docs.title: What is checked, and what is not
docs.text: The library rejects non-finite inputs, non-positive pressure and negative salinity, and H₂O–NaCl temperatures above 1273.15 K. It does not reject every input outside the published model domain (0–1000 °C, 1–5000 bar, X = 0–1): pressures below 1 bar are evaluated as extrapolations, and a salinity above 1, which is not physical, is evaluated too. Check your inputs against the domain; see Model and limitations.

docs.title: Evaluating states
docs.text:
Two functions evaluate the equation of state on scalars or NumPy arrays:

xthermo.tpx(model, T, p, X=0.0, *, errors="raise", absent="zero")   # temperature input
xthermo.hpx(model, H, p, X=0.0, *, errors="raise", absent="zero")   # enthalpy input
  • model is any model object: H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl(...), H2O.cIAPS84(), H2O.cIAPWS95() or NaCl.cNaCl(...).
  • T in K, p in Pa, H in J/kg, X in kg/kg. The water models ignore X.
  • The result is a xthermo.States object (below). hpx also returns the temperature, in T.
  • errors and absent choose how failed points and absent phases are reported: see Errors and status and Absent phases below.

docs.title: Scalars, arrays and broadcasting
docs.text:
The inputs can be numbers, lists or NumPy arrays of any shape that broadcast together. Every result array has the broadcast shape. A typical grid puts one input along each axis:

import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
T = np.linspace(100, 600, 6) + 273.15           # 6 temperatures, K
X = np.array([0.001, 0.032, 0.1, 0.3])          # 4 salinities, kg/kg

s = xthermo.tpx(sw, T[:, None], 300e5, X[None, :])
print(s.shape)                                  # (6, 4): temperature along axis 0, salinity along 1
print(s.Rho.round(1))                           # bulk density, kg/m³
print(s.phase_name[:, 1])                       # phases of 3.2 wt% NaCl from 100 to 600 °C

With scalar inputs every field is a single NumPy number:

import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, 573.15, 300e5, 0.1)          # 300 °C, 300 bar, 10 wt% NaCl
print(s.phase_name, round(float(s.Rho), 1), "kg/m³", round(float(s.H) / 1e6, 4), "MJ/kg")

All points are evaluated in one call into the C++ library. With the IAPS-84 backend a brine state takes a few microseconds; IAPWS-95 brines are slower (tenths of a millisecond), because the water equation of state is solved iteratively.

docs.title: The States result
docs.text:
Fields are read with attribute or key access, s.Rho or s["Rho"]; s.keys() lists them. Each field is a read-only NumPy array; use s.Rho.copy() for a writable one. Arrays stay valid after the model is deleted.

Attribute Content shape shape of the broadcast inputs fluid name of the model's fluid, e.g. "H2O-NaCl" phase phase-region code of each point (integer, table below) phase_name the name of each code, e.g. "V+L" (array of strings, or a string for scalar input) has(phase) mask: "liquid", "vapour" (or "vapor") or "halite" is present at an evaluated point status xthermo.Status of each point; Status.Ok for evaluated points (Errors and status) ok mask of the evaluated points (status == Status.Ok) failures list of (index, Status, message) for the points that were not evaluated

docs.title: Phase identification
docs.text:
phase holds the library's phase-region code. Its name is s.phase_name, or model.phase_name(code).

Code Name Phases present (has) 0 Liquid liquid 1 Vapor vapour 2 Solid halite (pure NaCl) 3, 4, 5 Supercritical, Sup.crit. vapor, Sup.crit. liquid one fluid phase, reported in the liquid fields (_l) 6 Critical point as 3 7 V+L(water) liquid, vapour (pure water at its boiling curve) 8 L+H liquid, halite 9 V+H vapour, halite 10 V+L liquid, vapour 11 V+L+H liquid, vapour, halite 12 Unknown none: the point was not evaluated

The labels "Liquid" and "Vapor" for a single-phase H₂O–NaCl fluid follow the library's classification. Above the critical curve of the mixture the fluid changes continuously between the two; there is no phase boundary there.

import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
T = np.linspace(300, 600, 7) + 273.15
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, T, 250e5, 0.032)             # seawater salinity, heated at 250 bar

two_phase = s.has("vapour") & s.has("liquid")    # where seawater has split into vapour and brine
print(T[two_phase] - 273.15)
print(s.X_l[two_phase], s.X_v[two_phase])        # brine and vapour salinity, kg/kg

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
Each property comes as a bulk value and, where it applies, as phase values with the suffixes _l (liquid), _v (vapour) and _h (halite). In a single-phase state the bulk value is the value of that phase.

Field Unit Meaning T, p, X K, Pa, kg/kg temperature, pressure, bulk salinity (T evaluated by hpx) H, H_l, H_v, H_h J/kg specific enthalpy Rho, Rho_l, Rho_v, Rho_h kg/m³ density Cp, Cp_l, Cp_v, Cp_h J/(kg K) isobaric heat capacity (∂h/∂T)p,X; phases at fixed composition Mu, Mu_l, Mu_v Pa s dynamic viscosity; NaN where the viscosity correlation does not evaluate S_l, S_v, S_h – phase saturations (below) X_l, X_v kg/kg salinity of the liquid and the vapour dRhodT, dRhodT_l, dRhodT_v kg/(m³ K) ∂ρ/∂T at fixed p dRhodP, dRhodP_l, dRhodP_v kg/(m³ Pa) ∂ρ/∂p at fixed T IsothermalCompressibility, IsothermalCompressibility_l, IsothermalCompressibility_v 1/Pa (1/ρ) ∂ρ/∂p at fixed T IsobaricExpansivity, IsobaricExpansivity_l, IsobaricExpansivity_v 1/K −(1/ρ) ∂ρ/∂T at fixed p

Multiphase states (V+L, V+H, L+H, V+L+H): Rho and H are the bulk values of the phase assemblage, and the saturations are volume fractions (the water models report the vapour mass fraction in their two-phase states). The bulk Cp contains no latent heat, the bulk Mu is not a mixture viscosity (use Mu_l and Mu_v), and some bulk derivatives are not computed. The definitions, and what the fields hold in each case, are on Model and limitations. Convert saturations to mass fractions with wi = Si ρi / ρ. The pure NaCl model reports its properties in the bulk fields only.

import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, 400 + 273.15, 250e5, 0.1)    # 400 °C, 250 bar, 10 wt% NaCl: vapour + liquid

w_v = s.S_v * s.Rho_v / s.Rho                     # vapour mass fraction from the volume fraction
print(s.phase_name, f"vapour: {float(s.S_v):.3f} of the volume, {float(w_v):.3f} of the mass")
print(f"liquid {float(s.X_l):.4f} kg/kg, {float(s.Rho_l):.1f} kg/m³")
print(f"vapour {float(s.X_v):.2e} kg/kg, {float(s.Rho_v):.1f} kg/m³")

docs.title: Absent phases
docs.text:
In the library's results the fields of a phase that is not present hold 0: Rho_v of a pure liquid, for example. That is the default, absent="zero". With absent="nan" these phase fields are NaN instead, which keeps absent phases out of plots and statistics:

import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
T = np.array([300.0, 400.0, 500.0]) + 273.15
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, T, 250e5, 0.032, absent="nan")
print(s.phase_name)                               # Liquid, V+L, V+H
print(s.Rho_v)                                    # NaN where there is no vapour
print(s.Rho_l)                                    # NaN where there is no liquid
print(s.S_v)                                      # saturations are never changed: 0 where absent

absent="nan" affects only the phase fields (_l, _v, _h, except the saturations) of the States result. Bulk fields and the library's own results are unchanged. Whether a phase is present follows the phase code; has() gives the same mask.

docs.title: Enthalpy-based input
docs.text:
hpx inverts the enthalpy: it finds the state with the given specific enthalpy, pressure and salinity, and returns it with its temperature.

import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
H = np.array([1.0e6, 2.0e6, 3.0e6])               # J/kg
s = xthermo.hpx(sw, H, 300e5, 0.05)               # 300 bar, 5 wt% NaCl
print(s.T - 273.15)                               # °C
print(s.phase_name)

The field H of the result is the enthalpy of the returned state. It agrees with the input to within the solver tolerance, except at X = 1 (pure NaCl in the H₂O–NaCl model) inside the melting range, where the returned state can have a different enthalpy (Under investigation). For plots on an enthalpy grid, use the input values as coordinates (see Property maps). The pure NaCl model has no enthalpy-based input (hpx raises NotAvailableError).

docs.title: Phase boundaries
docs.text:
The model object cH2ONaCl computes the phase boundaries of the H₂O–NaCl system directly: the three-phase surface V+L+H, the critical curve, the halite liquidus and the compositions of coexisting phases. For complete sections through the phase diagram use Phase diagrams; for properties on grids, Evaluating states. The Gallery shows how the phase diagram changes with pressure.

These functions take and return SI units (K, Pa, kg/kg). They accept NumPy arrays, but return tuples or lists: wrap the results in np.array(...), as in the examples below.

docs.title: 3-D overview
docs.text:
The full phase boundary structure in T–p–X space: the three-phase surface V+L+H, the V+H surface, the halite liquidus, the two limbs of the V+L region and the critical curve.

Code to reproduce this figure 
import warnings
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
from matplotlib.colors import to_hex
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)
sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")

# ── VLH surface (V→L side and L→H side) ──────────────────────────────────
nT = 80
nT_high = nT // 3
T_high  = H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH + (sw.Tmax_VLH() - H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH) * 0.95
T_vlh   = np.append(np.linspace(H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH, T_high, nT - nT_high),
                    np.linspace(T_high, sw.Tmax_VLH(), nT_high))
P_vlh   = np.array(sw.P_VLH(T_vlh))
Xl_vlh, Xv_vlh = np.array(sw.X_VLH(T_vlh, P_vlh))

n_log, n_lin = 20, 40
nX = n_log + n_lin
TT_vlh = np.tile(T_vlh, (nX, 1))
PP_vlh = np.tile(P_vlh, (nX, 1))
XX_V2L = np.zeros_like(TT_vlh)
XX_L2H = np.zeros_like(TT_vlh)
for j in range(len(T_vlh)):
    XX_V2L[:, j] = np.append(
        10 ** np.linspace(np.log10(max(Xv_vlh[j], 1e-10)), np.log10(0.01), n_log),
        np.linspace(0.01, Xl_vlh[j], n_lin))
    XX_L2H[:, j] = np.linspace(Xl_vlh[j], 1.0, nX)

# ── VH surface ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
nP = 60
T_vh = np.linspace(H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH, sw.Tmax_VLH(), nT)
P_vlh2 = np.array(sw.P_VLH(T_vh))
TT_vh = np.tile(T_vh, (nP, 1))
PP_vh = np.zeros_like(TT_vh)
np_low = nP // 3
for i in range(len(T_vh)):
    p_low = sw.pmin() + (P_vlh2[i] - sw.pmin()) * 0.1
    PP_vh[:, i] = np.append(np.linspace(sw.pmin(), p_low, np_low),
                            np.linspace(p_low, P_vlh2[i], nP - np_low))
XX_VH = np.array(sw.X_VH(TT_vh.ravel(), PP_vh.ravel())).reshape(TT_vh.shape)

# ── Halite liquidus ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
TT_lh = np.tile(T_vh, (nP, 1))
PP_lh = np.zeros_like(TT_lh)
for i in range(len(T_vh)):
    PP_lh[:, i] = np.linspace(P_vlh2[i], 2500e5, nP)
XL_LH = np.array(sw.X_HaliteLiquidus(TT_lh.ravel(), PP_lh.ravel())).reshape(TT_lh.shape)

# ── VL surfaces ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
pb_l = sw.PhaseBoundary_VL_DeformLinear(H2ONaCl.Liquid)
pb_v = sw.PhaseBoundary_VL_DeformLinear(H2ONaCl.Vapor)

# ── Critical curve ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
T_crit = np.linspace(sw.get_pWater().T_critical(), sw.Tmax(), 80)
p_crit, X_crit = np.array(sw.P_X_Critical(T_crit))

# ── Plot ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(12, 9))
ax  = fig.add_subplot(111, projection='3d', facecolor='None')
legend = []   # 3-D surfaces give no usable legend handles: one coloured swatch per surface

def surf(TT, PP, XX, color, label):
    ax.plot_surface(XX * 100, TT - 273.15, PP / 1e5,
                    color=color, alpha=0.45, linewidth=0)
    ax.plot_wireframe(XX * 100, TT - 273.15, PP / 1e5,
                      color=color, lw=0.4)
    legend.append(Patch(fc=color, ec=color, alpha=0.6, label=label))

surf(TT_vlh, PP_vlh, XX_V2L,  'steelblue', 'VLH (V side)')
surf(TT_vlh, PP_vlh, XX_L2H,  'orange',    'VLH (L+H side)')
surf(TT_vh,  PP_vh,  XX_VH,   'purple',    'VH surface')
surf(TT_lh,  PP_lh,  XL_LH,   'limegreen', 'Halite liquidus')

for pb, color, label in [(pb_l, 'black', 'VL liquid'), (pb_v, 'gray', 'VL vapor')]:
    T2 = np.array(pb.T); P2 = np.array(pb.p); X2 = np.array(pb.X)
    ax.plot_surface(X2 * 100, T2 - 273.15, P2 / 1e5, color=color, alpha=0.3, linewidth=0)
    ax.plot_wireframe(X2 * 100, T2 - 273.15, P2 / 1e5, color=color, lw=0.4)
    legend.append(Patch(fc=color, ec=color, alpha=0.4, label=label))

ax.plot(X_crit * 100, T_crit - 273.15, p_crit / 1e5, color='red', lw=2)
legend.append(Line2D([], [], color='red', lw=2, label='Critical curve'))
ax.plot(Xv_vlh * 100, T_vlh - 273.15, P_vlh / 1e5, color='red',   lw=1)
ax.plot(Xl_vlh * 100, T_vlh - 273.15, P_vlh / 1e5, color='green', lw=1)

ax.set_xlabel('Salinity (wt% NaCl)', fontsize=10, labelpad=8)
ax.set_ylabel('Temperature (°C)',    fontsize=10, labelpad=8)
ax.set_zlabel('Pressure (bar)',      fontsize=10, labelpad=8)
ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_ylim(0, 1000); ax.set_zlim(0, 2500)
ax.view_init(elev=25, azim=-145)
ax.set_title(r'H$_2$O–NaCl phase boundaries in T–p–X space', fontsize=13, pad=12)
ax.legend(handles=legend, loc='upper left', fontsize=9)
ax.set_box_aspect(None, zoom=0.88)   # leaves room for the axis labels
plt.show()

docs.title: The three-phase surface V+L+H
docs.text:
The three-phase vapour + liquid + halite (V+L+H) surface is parameterised by temperature. The left panel shows the coexistence pressure; the right panel shows the saturated liquid (halite liquidus) and vapour compositions along the surface.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")

T = np.linspace(H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH, H2ONaCl.T_MAX_VLH, 200)   # K
P_vlh = np.array(sw.P_VLH(T))                                  # Pa
XL_vlh, XV_vlh = np.array(sw.X_VLH(T, P_vlh))                 # kg/kg

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))

axes[0].plot(T - 273.15, P_vlh / 1e5)
axes[0].set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Pressure (bar)")
axes[0].set_title("VLH coexistence pressure")

axes[1].plot(T - 273.15, XL_vlh * 100, label="Liquid (halite liquidus)")
axes[1].plot(T - 273.15, XV_vlh * 100, label="Vapour")
axes[1].set_yscale("log")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Salinity (wt% NaCl)")
axes[1].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.title: Critical curve
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

from xthermo import H2O

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")

# the critical curve starts at the critical point of water
# (below it, P_X_Critical returns the boiling pressure of water, with X = 0)
T_c = H2O.cIAPS84().T_critical()               # K
T = np.linspace(T_c, sw.Tmax(), 200)           # K
P_crit, X_crit = np.array(sw.P_X_Critical(T))  # Pa, kg/kg

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(T - 273.15, P_crit / 1e5)
ax.set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)")
ax.set_ylabel("Critical pressure (bar)")
ax.set_title("H\u2082O\u2013NaCl critical curve")
plt.show()

docs.title: Phase compositions on the V+L+H surface and in V+L
docs.text:
Along the V+L+H surface, X_VLH returns the saturated liquid composition (the halite liquidus) and the saturated vapour composition. The surface ends at T_MAX_VLH ≈ 800.4 °C. T_MIN_VLH ≈ 107.8 °C is the temperature at which its pressure reaches 1 bar, the lower pressure limit of the model; at lower temperatures the surface lies below 1 bar.

The V+L two-phase region lies at pressures above the V+L+H pressure P_VLH and below the critical pressure. Below P_VLH, vapour coexists with halite (V+H). Above T_MAX_VLH, V+L is bounded from below by the NaCl boiling curve. Within V+L, XL_VL and XV_VL return the compositions of the coexisting liquid and vapour:

import numpy as np
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")

# along the V+L+H surface
T = np.linspace(400 + 273.15, 800 + 273.15, 5)    # K
P_vlh = np.array(sw.P_VLH(T))                      # Pa
XL_vlh, XV_vlh = np.array(sw.X_VLH(T, P_vlh))     # liquid (halite liquidus), vapour [kg/kg]

# inside V+L: 450 °C, 300 bar (P_VLH < p < P_crit)
T1, p1 = 450 + 273.15, 300e5
print(f"P_VLH = {sw.P_VLH(T1)/1e5:.1f} bar, P_crit = {sw.P_X_Critical(T1)[0]/1e5:.1f} bar")
print(f"X_liquid = {sw.XL_VL(T1, p1):.4f} kg/kg, X_vapour = {sw.XV_VL(T1, p1):.3e} kg/kg")

docs.title: Phase diagrams
docs.text:
The library computes the geometry of the phase regions of H₂O–NaCl along an isobar or an isotherm from its phase-boundary correlations:

Method Section Coordinates sw.Slice_constP(p) isobaric, at pressure p [Pa] T–X and H–X sw.Slice_constT(T) isothermal, at temperature T [K] P–X

Each result holds the polygons of the multiphase regions (V+L, V+H, L+H, V+L+H), their boundary lines and the invariant points, with names and colours. The plotting helpers draw them with Matplotlib (pip install ".[plotting]"). Unshaded areas are single-phase fluid. The axes are labelled in °C, bar, wt% NaCl and MJ/kg.

Because these diagrams draw the computed boundaries, they do not depend on a grid resolution (a few known inaccuracies are noted below). A grid of phase codes, by contrast, has staircase edges, and contour plots of it interpolate between categories that have no order. Use plot_phases (Property maps) only where no section is available, for example for pure water.

docs.title: A complete isobaric figure: plot_Pslice
docs.text:
xthermo.plot_Pslice(P0, x0_log_linear=0.01, sw=None) draws temperature (a) and specific enthalpy (b) against salinity at pressure P0. The salinity axis is logarithmic below x0_log_linear (kg/kg; 1 wt% by default) and linear above, with a strip for pure water (X = 0) on the left.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
r = xthermo.plot_Pslice(300e5, sw=sw)        # isobaric section at 300 bar: T-X (a) and H-X (b)
plt.show()

At 300 bar, above the critical pressure of water, the vapour + liquid region (pink) begins at the critical point of the mixture at about 408 °C. The vapour + halite region (grey) lies between the two temperatures of the three-phase assemblage V+L+H (484 and 692 °C), and liquid + halite (blue) bounds the salt-rich side. In the enthalpy section (b), V+L+H is not a line but a region (yellow, orange), because the phase proportions change at constant temperature.

plot_Pslice returns a dictionary: fig, data (the Slice_constP result), ax_T and ax_H (the log and linear halves of each panel), ax_water and handles (for a legend of your own).

docs.title: An isothermal figure: plot_Tslice
docs.text:
xthermo.plot_Tslice(T0, x0_log_linear=0.01, sw=None, plog=True) draws pressure against salinity at temperature T0, with a logarithmic pressure axis by default.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
r = xthermo.plot_Tslice(450 + 273.15, sw=sw)   # isothermal section at 450 °C: P-X
plt.show()

docs.title: Your own axes: plot_slice
docs.text:
xthermo.plot_slice(ax, section, x="X", y=None, regions=True, lines=True, points=True, legend=False) draws a section on Matplotlib axes you create, so you can combine it with other plots. x and y are "T", "P", "X" or "H"; y defaults to "T" for an isobaric and "P" for an isothermal section. ax can also be a list of axes. It returns {label: artist} for a legend.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
section = sw.Slice_constP(25e5)                  # the phase-region geometry at 25 bar

fig, (ax_t, ax_h) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.2), layout="constrained")
for ax in (ax_t, ax_h):
    ax.set_xscale("log")                         # salinity on a log axis
    ax.set_xlim(1e-4, 100)                       # wt% NaCl
handles = xthermo.plot_slice(ax_t, section, x="X", y="T")
xthermo.plot_slice(ax_h, section, x="X", y="H")
ax_t.set_ylim(0, 1000)
fig.legend(handles.values(), handles.keys(), loc="outside lower center", ncol=6, fontsize="small")
plt.show()

At 25 bar, below the critical pressure of water, there are two three-phase temperatures (242 °C and 794 °C), and vapour + halite covers most of the diagram between them.

Set the scale of the axes (ax.set_xscale("log")) before or after calling plot_slice; the polygons are drawn in data coordinates. Pure water, X = 0, cannot be shown on a log axis: plot_Pslice adds the strip for it.

Known limitations of the section geometry

The section geometry is checked against the equation of state point by point in the test suite, and agrees away from the boundaries. Three details of the library's geometry are known to be inaccurate: in isobaric H–X sections below about 221 bar a thin sliver of the vapour + liquid region at salinities below 0.13 wt% NaCl is missing; in isothermal sections the liquid + halite region continues below the three-phase pressure, where vapour + halite is stable (the plotting helpers draw vapour + halite on top, so the figure is correct); and isothermal sections below 374 °C contain a spurious "critical point" at X = 0. They are listed with the other known defects.

docs.title: Axis helpers
docs.text:
plot_Pslice and plot_Tslice are built from two helpers you can also use directly:

  • xthermo.makeLogLinearAxes(ax, width_logaxis=0.4, xlim_log=(2e-3, 1), xmax=100, ...) replaces ax by a salinity axis that is logarithmic up to xlim_log[1] wt% and linear above. It returns (ax_log, ax_linear); draw on both, e.g. plot_slice([ax_log, ax_linear], section).
  • xthermo.createWaterAxes(ax_log) adds the narrow strip for pure water at the left of the log axis.

docs.title: Property maps
docs.text:
Evaluate a grid with xthermo.tpx or xthermo.hpx, then draw it with two helpers (Matplotlib required):

xthermo.plot_property(ax, states, field, x="X", y="T", *, cmap="viridis", norm=None,
                      vmin=None, vmax=None, contours=None, contour_kw=None, colorbar=True,
                      failed="0.75", label=None)
xthermo.plot_phases(ax, states, x="X", y="T", *, legend=True, failed="0.75")
  • states must be a 2-D result: broadcast one input along each axis, e.g. T[:, None] and X[None, :].
  • x and y are "T", "P", "X" or "H". Axes are labelled in °C, bar, wt% NaCl and MJ/kg; the property and its colour bar stay in SI units.
  • Each point is one cell (pcolormesh); nothing is interpolated. On a logarithmic axis the cells are centred in log space, so set the axis scale to match your grid.
  • Points that were not evaluated (states.ok is False) are drawn in the colour failed (grey; None to leave them out). Evaluate with errors="nan" so that such points don't stop the grid.
  • Contours are drawn separately in each phase assemblage (liquid, vapour, V+L, L+H, V+H, V+L+H). A contour line therefore ends at a phase boundary instead of being interpolated across it, where many properties jump.
  • plot_property returns {"mesh", "contours", "colorbar", "failed"}; contours is a dict of contour sets keyed by assemblage. plot_phases returns {"mesh", "handles"}.

docs.title: A property map with section boundaries
docs.text:
The bulk density at 300 bar, with the boundaries of the phase regions drawn on top by plot_slice:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
T = np.linspace(1, 999, 250) + 273.15              # K
X = np.logspace(-5, 0, 250)                        # kg/kg
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, T[:, None], 300e5, X[None, :], errors="nan")   # a 250 x 250 grid at 300 bar

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.8), layout="constrained")
ax.set_xscale("log")
xthermo.plot_property(ax, s, "Rho", x="X", y="T", cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=1300,   # cap the colour scale
                      contours=np.arange(200, 1300, 200))
xthermo.plot_slice(ax, sw.Slice_constP(300e5), x="X", y="T", regions=False, points=False)  # boundaries on top
ax.set_title("Bulk density at 300 bar")
plt.show()

In the multiphase regions the map shows the bulk density of the phase assemblage (Σ Si ρi). Other bulk fields have restricted meanings there; check the field table before mapping Cp, Mu or the derivatives. Use phase fields such as Rho_l with absent="nan" to map a property of one phase only.

docs.title: Enthalpy grids
docs.text:
The H of an hpx result is the enthalpy of the returned state, which can differ slightly from the requested value (and, at X = 1, pure NaCl in the H₂O–NaCl model, inside the melting range substantially: Under investigation). So give the grid's enthalpy axis as the input values, y=("H", H), rather than reading it from the result:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
H = np.linspace(0.1e6, 4.4e6, 200)                 # J/kg
X = np.logspace(-4, 0, 200)                        # kg/kg
s = xthermo.hpx(sw, H[:, None], 250e5, X[None, :], errors="nan")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.8), layout="constrained")
ax.set_xscale("log")
xthermo.plot_property(ax, s, "T", x="X", y=("H", H), cmap="magma",       # H: the input values (see below)
                      contours=np.arange(100, 1000, 100) + 273.15, label="temperature (K)")
xthermo.plot_slice(ax, sw.Slice_constP(250e5), x="X", y="H", regions=False, points=False)
ax.set_xlim(1e-2, 100)                             # wt% NaCl: the grid (boundary lines reach X = 0)
ax.set_ylim(0, 4.6)                                # MJ/kg
ax.set_title("Temperature from H, p, X at 250 bar (grey: not evaluated)")
plt.show()

The grey area is where hpx did not evaluate: enthalpies above the enthalpy at the upper temperature limit of the model (1000 °C). The three-phase assemblage V+L+H, a line in temperature, is a band in enthalpy (between the orange lines), and temperature is constant across it.

docs.title: Phase maps
docs.text:
plot_phases colours each point by its phase code, with a legend of phase names. Use it where no section geometry exists, as for pure water in temperature and pressure:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import xthermo
from matplotlib.colors import LogNorm
from xthermo import H2O

water = H2O.cIAPS84()
T = np.linspace(280, 1000, 250)                    # K
p = np.geomspace(1e5, 1000e5, 250)                 # Pa
s = xthermo.tpx(water, T[None, :], p[:, None], errors="nan")

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.2), layout="constrained")
for ax in (ax1, ax2):
    ax.set_yscale("log")
xthermo.plot_phases(ax1, s, x="T", y="P")
xthermo.plot_property(ax2, s, "Rho", x="T", y="P", norm=LogNorm(),
                      contours=[1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300, 600, 800, 1000])
ax1.set_title("Phase (IAPS-84 water)")
ax2.set_title("Density")
plt.show()

The density contours stop at the boiling curve, where liquid and vapour meet and the density jumps. They also stop where the library's label changes from "Vapor" to a supercritical code at the critical pressure, which is not a physical boundary.

docs.title: Water
docs.text:
xthermo.H2O has two equations of state for pure water:

Class Formulation H2O.cIAPS84() IAPS-84 (Haar, Gallagher & Kell 1984), computed with PROST 4.1. The reference backend of the Driesner H₂O–NaCl model H2O.cIAPWS95() IAPWS-95 (Wagner & Pruß 2002)

They are evaluated with xthermo.tpx and xthermo.hpx like the brine model; X is ignored.

import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2O

water = H2O.cIAPS84()
T = np.array([20.0, 200.0, 400.0]) + 273.15                 # K
s = xthermo.tpx(water, T, 250e5)                            # 250 bar
print(s.phase_name)
print(s.Rho, "kg/m³")
print(s.Mu, "Pa s")

At pressures above the critical pressure of water (220.5 bar with IAPS-84, 220.6 bar with IAPWS-95), the library labels a fluid below the critical temperature "Sup.crit. liquid" and one above it "Supercritical".

In the two-phase states of the water models, S_v is the vapour mass fraction (quality), not a volume fraction as in H₂O–NaCl. See Evaluating states.

docs.title: Saturation
docs.text:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from xthermo import H2O

water = H2O.cIAPS84()

T = np.linspace(water.Tmin(), water.T_critical(), 100)   # K
p_boil = np.array([water.Boiling_p(Ti) for Ti in T])     # Pa

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(T - 273.15, p_boil / 1e5)
ax.plot(water.T_critical() - 273.15, water.p_critical() / 1e5,
        'ro', label=f"Critical point ({water.T_critical()-273.15:.1f} °C)")
ax.set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)")
ax.set_ylabel("Saturation pressure (bar)")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.legend()
plt.show()

Boiling_p(T) gives the saturation pressure and Boiling_T(p) the saturation temperature. Boiling_p_props(T) returns the saturated liquid and vapour:

from xthermo import H2O

water = H2O.cIAPS84()

T = 300 + 273.15   # K
prop = water.Boiling_p_props(T)

print(f"Saturation pressure: {prop.p/1e5:.2f} bar")
print(f"Liquid density:      {prop.Rho_l:.1f} kg/m³")
print(f"Vapour density:      {prop.Rho_v:.3f} kg/m³")
print(f"Boiling point at 1 bar: {water.Boiling_T(1e5) - 273.15:.2f} °C")

The IAPWS-95 class has the same methods: water = H2O.cIAPWS95(). Exactly on the saturation curve, IAPWS-95 water evaluated with tpx raises NotConvergedError; evaluate slightly off it, or use the saturation functions.

docs.text:
xthermo.NaCl.cNaCl("IAPS84") is the pure NaCl model of Driesner (2007): halite (solid) and liquid NaCl, with their melting, sublimation and boiling curves. Its liquid properties are the Driesner brine correlations at X = 1, which use a water equation of state; the argument selects it.

import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import NaCl

nacl = NaCl.cNaCl("IAPS84")
print(f"melting point at 1 bar: {nacl.Melting_T(1e5) - 273.15:.1f} °C")

T = np.array([500.0, 900.0]) + 273.15
s = xthermo.tpx(nacl, T, 1e5)                       # X is ignored
print(s.phase_name)                                 # ['Solid' 'Liquid']
print(s.Rho, "kg/m³")

The NaCl model reports its properties in the bulk fields only (Rho, H, Cp, …). It has no enthalpy-based input: hpx raises NotAvailableError. The properties of pure NaCl have not been independently verified in the review of xThermo; see Model and limitations.
